egypt_wide_estimate.text: For an Egyptian town with no evidence of its own after the Arab conquest, the end of Greek speech is put at c. 750 (range 650-850). Across Egypt, Greek private letters and contracts of Christians become rare after the conquest and end in the 8th century; Greek lasted longest in accounts and in the formulae of Coptic documents, and the townspeople wrote Coptic, which Arabic later replaced. Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi), though Greek fiscal documents went on for some decades.
egypt_wide_estimate.markers: Greek private letters and contracts of Christians thin out after the 640s and end in the 8th century; Greek registers until the order of 705/706 (al-Kindi); Greek letters of the governor Qurra ibn Sharik (709-714) to the pagarch at Aphrodito; Greek accounts in the Fayum into the second half of the 8th century; Greek-Arabic protocols on papyrus rolls from the reign of the caliph 'Abd al-Malik (685-705); Greek invocations, dating formulae and witness subscriptions in Coptic legal documents of the 8th century (Bagnall 1993; Fournet 2009; Papaconstantinou 2010; Sijpesteijn 2013).
egypt_wide_estimate.exceptions: Alexandria c. 850 (750-950), for its Melkite community; Aphrodito c. 720 (710-780); towns abandoned at a known date; Cyrenaica, where no Greek text by a resident is known after 643.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: Alexandria (centre: Kom el-Dikka, the Eastern Harbour, Kom el-Shuqafa), Alexandria Governorate
cities.nome: none (polis outside the nomes; its chora included the Mareotes)
cities.greek_from_text: founded by Alexander the Great, early 331 BC (Arr. Anab. 3.1.5-3.2.2; Plut. Alex. 26; the Alexander Romance 1.32 gives the day as 25 Tybi); laid out by Deinokrates; capital of the Ptolemies from c. 313 BC
cities.until_text: Administration: 'Amr ibn al-'As took the city by the treaty signed by the patriarch Cyrus (November 641); the Roman garrison and many Greek-speaking residents sailed away in September 642; after Manuel's reoccupation (645/646) 'Amr retook it by storm and razed its walls (646). Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 705/706 (order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik, al-Kindi). Speech: a Chalcedonian (Melkite) community stayed, the part of the population most likely to keep Greek; its see was vacant for most of c. 650-727 and was restored under Cosmas I (c. 727-768), whose church was again in communion with the Greek-speaking patriarchates (Theophanes, under 742/743). No dated Greek letter, contract or epitaph of an Alexandrian resident is known after the 7th c. By the 10th c. the Melkites of Egypt wrote Arabic: Patriarch Eutychius (Sa'id ibn Bitriq, born in Fustat 877, patriarch 933-940) wrote his Annals in Arabic and seems not to have known Greek. Greek remained the Melkite liturgical language, which does not extend the phase. The end of Greek speech is therefore placed c. 850 (750-950), later than the Egypt-wide estimate because of the Melkite community of the capital. Greek merchants and clergy from the empire in later centuries are newcomers.
cities.fade_evidence: Emigration under the treaty of 641/642; Greek administration in Egypt to 705/706, with Greek-Arabic protocols and Greek fiscal documents into the 8th c.; Melkite see vacant c. 650-727, restored under Cosmas I (c. 727-768); Theophanes records the Alexandrian church's union with the other Chalcedonian patriarchates in 742/743; Melkite historiography in Arabic by the 10th c. (Eutychius, born 877, patriarch 933-940, who used Greek works only in translation); Greek kept as a liturgical language; Coptic and Arabic replaced Greek among the rest of the population.
cities.ended_by: Taken by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 641 (treaty with the patriarch Cyrus), evacuated by the Roman army 642; stormed again by 'Amr after Manuel's revolt, 646, walls razed. Afterwards the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi), which ended Greek in government but was not a ban on speech; no act against Greek speech is recorded: the evidence shows emigration and a shift of the remaining Melkites to Arabic by the 10th c. Earlier blows: Ptolemy VIII's expulsion of scholars and massacres (145 BC and after); Caracalla's massacre of the youth (215, Cass. Dio 78.22-23); Aurelian's destruction of the Brucheion (272, after Zenobia's occupation and the revolt of Firmus); Diocletian's siege and sack after the revolt of Domitius Domitianus and Achilleus (297/298); the Persian conquest under Shahrbaraz (619).

sources: Carrez-Maratray, Peluse et l'angle oriental du delta (1999)

cities.site: Faqus, Sharqia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: metropolis of the Arabian nome in Ptolemy (c. 150); Strabo (17.1.26) still calls it a village
cities.until_text: Administration Roman to 640/641, then Arab. Speech: no Greek evidence after the 7th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the district fell to 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641, after Pelusium and Bilbeis. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.pre_greek_note: Faqus continues the ancient name; an Egyptian form is not securely attested.
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Arabian nome (Ptolemy); the see 'Arabia' of Augustamnica II
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Arabian nome (Ptol. Geog. 4.5.53); see 'Arabia' (Hierocles 728)
cities.note: Phakoussa has also been placed at Tell Faqus or near Qantir; the late antique see is called 'Arabia'.

cities.site: Tell Mahrad, Wadi Feiran oasis, South Sinai Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: first attested as a see: bishop Netras, a disciple of abba Silvanus, c. 400 (Apophthegmata Patrum)
cities.until_text: Bishops to the 7th c. (Theodore of Pharan, Greek theologian, condemned in 680/681 as a Monothelete); after the Arab conquest of Sinai in the 630s-640s the town declined. The Greek-speaking monks of the fortified monastery of Sinai were a monastic community largely recruited from outside and do not extend the town's phase. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850). Here the townspeople went over to Arabic.
cities.fade_evidence: Theodore of Pharan wrote Greek theology (c. 620-640); no Greek evidence for the town later. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act: Sinai passed to the Arabs in the 630s-640s; the town shrank in the following centuries. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.pre_greek_note: Nabataean inscriptions of Sinai may name the oasis; not used here.
cities.bilingual_evidence: see with Greek-writing bishops (Netras c. 400; Theodore, 7th c.); episcopal church with Greek inscriptions (Grossmann's excavations); local Saracen (Arab) population
cities.status_evidence: see of Palaestina Tertia (bishops from c. 400 to the 7th c.); Pharan in Ptolemy, Geog. 5.17
cities.note: A desert see with a mostly Arab population; the Greek-speaking community may have been only clergy and monks, which would rule it out.

cities.site: Horbeit, near Abu Kebir, Sharqia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: metropolis of the Pharbaithite nome under Rome (Ptolemy 4.5); gymnasial order of the metropoleis from AD 4/5; boule from 200/201
cities.until_text: Administration Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: no Greek evidence after the 7th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop Arbethion (325) and later bishops. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.pre_greek_note: Horbeit is usually identified with Shedenu, capital of the 11th Lower Egyptian nome; the Greek name itself may come from an Egyptian Per-Horbeit.
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Pharbaithite nome; nome coins; bishop Arbethion at Nicaea 325
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Pharbaithite nome; see (Nicaea 325); Hierocles 728

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: El-Arish, North Sinai Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Hellenistic town on new ground (no earlier occupation found at El-Arish); a city on the border of Egypt and Syria in Strabo (16.2.31) and Diodorus (1.60)
cities.until_text: Bishops from the 4th c. (Melas under Valens, Sozomen 6.31; Hermogenes at Ephesus 431); the town fell to the Arabs on 'Amr's march into Egypt, 639/640, and survived as al-Arish. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850). Here the townspeople went over to Arabic.
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop Hermogenes (431), sent by Cyril of Alexandria to Rome; no Greek evidence after the 7th c. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The coast road fell to the Arabs when 'Amr ibn al-'As marched from Palestine on Pelusium, winter 639/640 (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam); the towns of the coast declined thereafter. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.pre_greek_note: The legend of nose-cut exiles (Diodorus 1.60; Strabo 16.2.31) is not evidence of an earlier town.
cities.status_evidence: city in Strabo and Diodorus; Hierocles 727; see (Melas, Solon; Hermogenes at Ephesus 431)
cities.note: Population probably mixed (Greek, Egyptian, Idumaean and Arab); Greek counted as the main civic language for lack of evidence of another.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: Samannud, Gharbia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Manetho, priest of Sebennytos, wrote his history of Egypt in Greek for Ptolemy II, c. 280 BC
cities.until_text: Administration Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: the Greek-speaking metropolitan class is not attested after the 7th c.; the town became Coptic- and then Arabic-speaking. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops of Sebennytos in late antiquity and later Coptic bishops. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Manetho of Sebennytos wrote his Aegyptiaca in Greek (c. 280 BC); metropolis of the Sebennyte nome with the Roman metropolitan order; see
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Sebennyte nome (Strabo 17.1.19; nome coins); see; Hierocles
cities.note: Manetho shows a Greek-educated priest rather than a Greek community; the Greek civic class is presumed from the metropolis status.

cities.site: Tell Hebua (with Tell Abu Sefa), about 4 km north-east of El-Qantara East, Ismailia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: first attested as a see: bishop Alypius at the Council of Ephesus, 431
cities.until_text: Known only from one bishop, in 431; no later evidence. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop Alypius (431); nothing later. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act; the eastern frontier fell to 'Amr ibn al-'As at the start of the conquest (Pelusium, 639-640). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.pre_greek_note: the frontier fortress of Tjaru of the New Kingdom (Tell Hebua)
cities.bilingual_evidence: see with bishop Alypius at the Council of Ephesus, 431 (Worp 1994); a fort and road station on the road from Pelusium into Egypt (Itinerarium Antonini; Notitia Dignitatum, an ala at Sele)
cities.status_evidence: see (Alypius at Ephesus 431; Worp 1994); suffragan of Pelusium in Augustamnica I; Roman fort (Notitia Dignitatum)
cities.note: A frontier fortress and road station whose see is known from one bishop. The garrison does not count; a Greek-speaking civilian community is only inferred from the see, as for the other see-only towns. Doubtful case.
sources: Worp, ZPE 100 (1994), checklist of bishops of Egypt AD 325 - c. 750
Acts of the Council of Ephesus (431), lists of bishops

cities.site: Damietta (the old town lay nearer the sea; it was razed and rebuilt inland in 1250), Damietta Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: first attested as a see: bishop at the council of Ephesus, 431
cities.until_text: Administration Roman to 641/642, then Arab; the population was Coptic-speaking Christian and then Arabic. Greek raids on Damietta (853 and later) did not restore Greek speech. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Four bishops known from 431 to 879 (Le Quien). Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek; the town was taken by an Arab detachment sent by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 641/642 (later Arabic tradition). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.pre_greek_note: Coptic Tamiati; an earlier Egyptian form is not securely attested.
cities.bilingual_evidence: see with bishops from 431; city in Stephanus of Byzantium
cities.status_evidence: see (bishop at Ephesus 431); Stephanus of Byzantium s.v.
cities.note: A small town in late antiquity; it became important only in the Arab period.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: San el-Hagar, Sharqia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Ptolemaic Greek inscriptions and Greek administration of the Tanite nome, 3rd c. BC
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: the Greek-speaking metropolitan class is the last attested in the 6th-7th c.; Tanis shrank in the Arab period, but Coptic bishops of Tanis are known into the Middle Ages, so the population turned Coptic and then Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishops of Tanis at the councils (325 onwards); later Coptic bishops. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Tanite nome; Ptolemaic Greek inscriptions (the bilingual Canopus decree of 238 BC was found here, 1866); Ptolemaic and Roman town (Petrie's excavations); bishop Tiberius at Nicaea 325
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Tanite nome; nome coins under Trajan and Hadrian; see (bishop Tiberius at Nicaea 325); Hierocles 726
cities.note: Capital of the 21st and 22nd dynasties; the Greek-period town occupied part of the old tell.

cities.site: Tell Tinnis, island in Lake Manzala, south-west of Port Said, Port Said Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: island town and see visited by John Cassian (c. 395), who found its bishop just dead
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman to 641/642, then Arab. Speech: the town grew under the Arabs into a great linen centre with a mostly Christian (Coptic-speaking) population; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Bishop Heron (451); the monk Bernard found the people nearly all Christians c. 870. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek; the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Much later Saladin had the civilian town evacuated (1192/93), and the remaining fort was razed after the Fifth Crusade (1220s). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.bilingual_evidence: see with bishops (Heron, condemned at Chalcedon 451); city in Hierocles; Roman-period tombs on the island
cities.status_evidence: Hierocles 727; see suffragan of Pelusium (bishop at Chalcedon 451)

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: Tell Timai, near Tmai el-Amdid, Dakahlia Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek mosaic signed by Sophilos with the portrait of Berenike II, c. 200 BC (Alexandria, Graeco-Roman Museum)
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: a Greek-educated civic class to late antiquity (Phileas, a rich man who had held civic offices, wrote in Greek; Serapion wrote Greek theology); later the bishops of Thmuis appear in Coptic sources. Greek probably faded in the 8th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Phileas' Greek letter (Eus. HE 8.10); Serapion's Greek works and the Euchologion; late Roman finds on site. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Phileas of Thmuis was executed in the persecution of Diocletian, c. 306 (Eus. HE 8.9-10). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.pre_greek_note: Coptic Thmoui; an Egyptian form is not securely attested.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Hellenistic mosaics signed in Greek by Sophilos (c. 200 BC); Greek tax rolls of the town (P. Thmouis 1, 2nd c. AD, found on site); the bishops and Greek writers Phileas (d. c. 306) and Serapion (c. 339-360)
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Mendesian (later Thmuite) nome in Roman times; boule; see (Phileas d. c. 306; a bishop at Nicaea 325; Serapion c. 339-360; Ptolemaeus at Seleucia 359; Aristobulus at Ephesus 431); Hierocles 726
cities.note: Grew beside Mendes and replaced it as the nome capital in the Roman period.
sources: Littman and Silverstein, Tell Timai project

cities.site: Sheikh Ibada, Mallawi district, Minya Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Founded by Hadrian in the autumn of 130 where Antinous drowned in the Nile (Cassius Dio 69.11; Antinoite papyri).
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: Antinoe remained a see and a town until it was abandoned around the 10th c., but its late texts are Coptic and Arabic; the Greek-speaking element faded in the 7th-8th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Seat of the governors of the Thebaid in the 6th c. (Dioscorus of Aphrodito wrote Greek poems and documents here); buildings of the Colluthus shrine in use to about the Arab conquest; later Coptic and Arabic writing exercises and a Coptic funerary stele dated 871. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Occupied by the Persians (619-629); the Thebaid passed to the Arabs under the treaty of Alexandria concluded with 'Amr ibn al-'As (641); the registers were put into Arabic in 705/706 under the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
cities.pre_greek_note: A temple of Ramesses II and an earlier settlement lay at the site; it is often identified with the Hermopolite town Hir-wer, which is not certain.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Founded with Greek settlers (many from Ptolemais Hermiou) under laws modelled on Naukratis, with tribes and demes, a boule and the Antinoeia games; from the 5th-6th c. a large Coptic-speaking Christian population (cult of St Colluthus, Coptic petitions and texts) beside the Greek civic and governing elite of the capital of the Thebaid
cities.status_evidence: Greek polis founded by Hadrian (130) with boule, prytanis and Antinoite citizenship; home of the 4th-c. mathematician Serenus; see with bishops from 325 (Tyrannos, Loukios), later metropolitan see; capital of the Thebaid from the 4th c.; Hierocles (Thebaid)

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: Atfih, Giza Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek settlers and Greek documents of the Aphroditopolite nome from the mid-3rd c. BC (Ptolemaic papyri, including the Zenon archive).
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: the town shifted to Coptic and then Arabic in the 7th-8th c.; no local evidence dates the end more closely. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Listed with Nilopolis in a 7th-c. Greek levy account of the cities of Arcadia (SB I 5337); few later Greek documents from the town; Coptic see of Petpeh continued after the conquest. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
cities.pre_greek_note: Temple of Hathor and a cow necropolis at the site.
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Aphroditopolite nome; Greek papyri naming its residents from the Ptolemaic period on; city of Arcadia in Hierocles; see
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Aphroditopolite nome; Hierocles (Arcadia); see with bishops Theodoros (before 339), Serenos (339), Chrysaorios (431)
cities.note: Greek civic life here is known mostly from its status as a nome metropolis; local Greek texts are few.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.other_names: Krokodilon polis, 'Krokodilopolis' (Greek, earlier name); Ptolemais Euergetis (Greek, Ptolemaic and Roman official name); Shedet (Egyptian); Piom (Coptic, also the name of the Fayum)
cities.site: Kiman Faris (Kom Faris), Medinet el-Fayum, Faiyum Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek cleruchs settled in the newly drained Fayum under Ptolemy II from the 260s BC; the nome was named Arsinoite after Arsinoe II by c. 257 BC and Krokodilopolis was its metropolis.
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: Greek survived in the Fayum mainly as a language of accounts into the second half of the 8th c.; Coptic took over private and legal documents in the 7th-8th c. and Arabic followed. Greek as a spoken language of residents probably ended before the last Greek accounts.
cities.fade_evidence: Pahlavi papyri from the Fayum under the Persian occupation (619-629); Greek and Greek-Arabic documents of the Arsinoite pagarchy under the Umayyads; Greek accounting documents from the Fayum (Vienna fragments, Naqlun) into the second half of the 8th c.; Coptic dominant thereafter.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The Fayum was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and fell to the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641 after the Roman commander John was killed (John of Nikiu, ch. 111-112); the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi).
cities.pre_greek_note: Modern 'Fayum' continues Coptic Piom, from Egyptian pa-yom 'the lake', a name of the region and later of the city.
cities.bilingual_evidence: gymnasium and gymnasial class from the Ptolemaic period; the privileged '6,475 Greek men' (katoikoi) of the nome in the Roman period; boule from 200/201; thousands of Greek letters, contracts and literary papyri of residents; Demotic temple and private documents beside them
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Arsinoite nome; gymnasium (Ptolemaic papyri); boule from 200/201; Christian teachers here debated with Dionysius of Alexandria c. 255 (Eus. HE 7.24); see with bishops from 325 (Melas) to Abraamios (c. 740); Hierocles (Arcadia)
cities.note: Kept as a bilingual city: the Greek settler element was unusually large, but Egyptian priests, Demotic contracts and later Coptic show that Greek was not the language of the whole town.

cities.other_names: Babylon (Coptic); Babalyun, Qasr al-Sham' (Arabic); Kheriaha (Egyptian, earlier settlement nearby)
cities.site: Qasr al-Sham', Old Cairo, Cairo Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Fortress by the Nile canal from Trajan's time (Amnis Traianus), rebuilt under Diocletian c. 300; first attested as a see with bishop Kyros at the council of Ephesus in 449.
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: the Greek-speaking part of the population (officials, Chalcedonian clergy, merchants) shrank after 641 and was absorbed into the Coptic- and then Arabic-speaking population of Fustat.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek remained the chancery language of the Arab governors at Fustat beside Babylon until 705/706; Greek-Arabic protocols and bilingual documents of the Umayyad period; Coptic and then Arabic took over in the churches of the fortress.
cities.ended_by: The fortress surrendered to 'Amr ibn al-'As after a siege of about seven months (December 640 or April 641; John of Nikiu); the Arab camp-city Fustat was founded beside it (641/642); the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). No act against Greek speech is recorded.
cities.pre_greek_note: The Egyptian settlement Kheriaha lay nearby; its exact relation to the Roman fortress town is not certain.
cities.bilingual_evidence: a large late Roman fortress town with churches, clergy and officials; see from the 5th c.; Greek-speaking officials and soldiers are well attested, a Greek-speaking civic body of residents much less clearly
cities.status_evidence: Roman fortress (Strabo 17.1.30; Notitia Dignitatum); see with bishops Kyros (449), Photios (459), Zosimos (c. 560), Theodoros (c. 743), Konstantinos (c. 755)
cities.note: City status rests on the see and the size of the town; Greek speakers attested here are mostly officials and soldiers. Later see lists put it under Leontopolis (Augustamnica II) rather than Arcadia; Delta listings may also claim it.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.other_names: Qs (Egyptian, per Trismegistos; older works give Saka or Hardai); Kais / Koeis (Coptic); el-Qays (Arabic)
cities.site: El-Qays, Beni Mazar district, Minya Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek settlers and documents of the Kynopolite nome from the Ptolemaic period; firm civic evidence only in the Roman period.
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: with few documents from the town itself, the end is placed with the general shift of Middle Egypt to Coptic and Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Few late Greek documents from the town; Coptic Kais survives as Arabic el-Qays. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
cities.pre_greek_note: Trismegistos gives Egyptian Qs, the source of Coptic Kais and Arabic el-Qays; older works call the capital of the 17th Upper Egyptian nome Saka or Hardai, and which lay under the Roman metropolis is debated.
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Kynopolite nome; Greek papyri of the nome; city of Arcadia in Hierocles; see
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Kynopolite nome; Hierocles (Arcadia); see with bishops from 325 (Aiglon, Adamantios) to Gregorios (c. 680)
cities.note: The Roman metropolis is usually put at el-Qays on the west bank; the dog necropolis is on the east bank near Hamatha. Distinct from Kynopolis in the Delta.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: Ihnasya el-Medina (Kom el-Aqarib), Beni Suef Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek settlers and Greek documents of residents of the Herakleopolite from the mid-3rd c. BC (Hibeh papyri).
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: Greek documents of the Herakleopolite pagarchy continue into the 8th c., mostly as administration and accounts; the residents of the town (Ahnas) went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
cities.fade_evidence: One of the earliest dated Arabic papyri is a Greek-Arabic receipt of 25 April 643 from Herakleopolis for sheep handed by the agents of the pagarchs Theodorakios and Christophoros to 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir and his troops (PERF 558); bilingual Greek-Arabic documents of the pagarchy in the Umayyad period; an 8th-c. Greek account found at Naqlun probably comes from the Herakleopolite; Coptic dominant afterwards.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek cleruchs in the nome from the 3rd c. BC; a Greek-speaking Jewish politeuma at Herakleopolis (papyri of 144-132 BC); gymnasial class; boule from 200/201; Greek papyri of residents into the Arab period
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Herakleopolite nome; gymnasial class; boule from 200/201; see with bishops from 325 (Petros); Hierocles (Arcadia)
sources: Cowey & Maresch, Urkunden des Politeuma der Juden von Herakleopolis (2001)

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: El-Ashmunein, Mallawi district, Minya Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek cavalry settlers of the Hermopolite dedicated a sanctuary to Ptolemy III and Berenike II (246-221 BC) in the city.
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: Greek and Greek-Arabic documents of the Hermopolite continue into the 8th c.; the medieval town el-Ashmunein was Coptic-speaking and later Arabic-speaking (its 10th-c. bishop Severus wrote in Arabic).
cities.fade_evidence: Pahlavi papyri from Hermopolis under the Persian occupation (619-629); Greek and bilingual documents of the Hermopolite pagarchy under the Umayyads; Coptic dominant in private documents from the 7th-8th c.; Severus ibn al-Muqaffa', bishop of el-Ashmunein, writing in Arabic in the 10th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and passed to the Arabs with the rest of Upper Egypt under the treaty of Alexandria concluded with 'Amr ibn al-'As (641); the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
cities.bilingual_evidence: Ptolemaic sanctuary dedicated to Ptolemy III and Berenike II by the cavalry settlers of the nome; gymnasium and gymnasial class; boule from 200/201 with a large council archive; thousands of Greek papyri of residents into the Arab period
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Hermopolite nome; gymnasium; boule from 200/201; see with bishops from 325 (Phasileus); Hierocles (Thebaid)
cities.note: In the Heptanomia until Diocletian, then in the Thebaid (Lower Thebaid).
sources: Wace, Megaw & Skeat, Hermopolis Magna: The Ptolemaic Sanctuary and the Basilica (1959)

cities.site: Ausim, Giza Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: nome metropolis under Rome: the Greek-speaking metropolite and gymnasial class was registered in every metropolis from AD 4/5 (boule from 200/201); no earlier town-specific Greek evidence found; metropolis of the Letopolite nome; Hierocles (Arcadia); see with bishops Isaak (325), Gamul (c. 728), Moses (c. 735)
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: with very few documents from the town, the end can only be placed with the general shift of Middle Egypt to Coptic and Arabic in the 7th-8th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Letopolite nome still a fiscal district in a 7th-c. Greek levy account of Arcadia (SB I 5337); no dated late Greek texts of residents; Coptic see of Boushem continued after the conquest. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
cities.pre_greek_note: Coptic Boushem / Oushem and Arabic Ausim continue it.
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Letopolite nome in the Roman period (Ptolemy, Geography 4.5); still a fiscal district in a 7th-c. Greek account of Arcadia; city of Arcadia in Hierocles; see; few Greek documents of residents survive
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Letopolite nome; Hierocles (Arcadia); see with bishops Isaak (325), Gamul (c. 728), Moses (c. 735)
cities.note: Lies at the apex of the Delta and may also be claimed for Lower Egypt; Greek-speaking residents are inferred from its status as a metropolis more than shown by local texts.

cities.other_names: Men-nefer and Inbu-hedj, 'White Walls' (Egyptian); Menfe / Memfi (Coptic); Manf (medieval Arabic)
cities.site: Mit Rahina, Badrashin district, Giza Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Ionian and Carian soldiers moved by Amasis (570-526 BC) from the Stratopeda to Memphis as his guard (Hdt. 2.154); their descendants are the Hellenomemphites of later documents. Bilingual civic body under the Ptolemies and Romans.
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: Memphis lost its people to the new Arab capital Fustat beside Babylon (founded 641/642) and was quarried for its stone; the Greek-speaking element faded in the 7th-8th c. while the Christian population kept Coptic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and papyri of Memphis run into the 6th-7th c.; the town was a see (the Melitian leader John Arkaph was its bishop, c. 330s) and remained a Coptic see after the conquest; Fustat drew away its population from 641/642; Arabic replaced Greek in the registers in 705/706. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Memphis was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and fell to the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As with the surrender of Babylon (640/641); the founding of Fustat (641/642) and the later removal of its stone for Fustat and Cairo emptied the town; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi).
cities.pre_greek_note: Also called Inbu-hedj, 'White Walls' (Egyptian).
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek quarter of the Hellenomemphites with its Hellenion from the 6th c. BC (Hdt. 2.154; Ptolemaic papyri); Greek letters of residents such as the Serapeum archive of Ptolemaios son of Glaukias (2nd c. BC, beside Demotic); nome metropolis with a gymnasial class and, from 200/201, a boule
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Memphite nome; Hellenomemphites and Hellenion; boule from 200/201; see by the early 4th c. (Antiochos, 325; the Melitian John Arkaph, 325-335); bishop Ptolemaios c. 700; Hierocles (Arcadia)
cities.note: Greeks were a minority quarter here from the 6th c. BC; the bilingual civic body is Ptolemaic and Roman. Phase start is the settlement under Amasis, not a civic foundation.
sources: Thompson, Memphis under the Ptolemies (2nd ed. 2012)

cities.other_names: Tilothis and Neilos (Greek); Tiloj / Telaj (Coptic); Dalas (Arabic)
cities.site: Dalas, Beni Suef Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: First evidence of a civic community: Chaeremon, aged bishop of Nilopolis, fled in the Decian persecution c. 250 (Dionysius of Alexandria in Eus. HE 6.42.3).
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek ended in the registers in 705/706 (al-Kindi). Speech: no local Greek evidence after the 6th-7th c.; the town shifted to Coptic and then Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Its district was separate in the 4th-5th c., merged with Herakleopolis by 538 and separate again for taxes by the late 6th c.; listed with Aphroditopolis in a 7th-c. Greek levy account of Arcadia (SB I 5337); seat of a pagarchy in the later 8th c.; Coptic Tiloj survives as Arabic Dalas. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
cities.pre_greek_note: Egyptian form given in modern reference works; Greek Tilothis, Coptic Tiloj and Arabic Dalas continue it.
cities.bilingual_evidence: see with a bishop by c. 250 (Chaeremon, Eus. HE 6.42.3); city of Arcadia in Hierocles; chief place of a toparchy of the Herakleopolite
cities.status_evidence: see by c. 250 (Chaeremon, Eus. HE 6.42.3), then Theon (325), Eusebios (431); Hierocles (Arcadia); Ptolemy 4.5 (on an island in the Nile)
cities.note: Not a nome metropolis; its Greek-speaking community is shown mainly by its early see. Placed at Dalas by the Coptic name; Ptolemy puts it on a Nile island.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.other_names: Per-Medjed (Egyptian); Pemdje (Coptic); Nea Ioustinou polis (Greek honorific name after an emperor Justin, 6th c.); el-Bahnasa (Arabic)
cities.site: El-Bahnasa, Beni Mazar district, Minya Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek cleruchs and Greek documents of residents of the Oxyrhynchite nome from the mid-3rd c. BC (Hibeh papyri).
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: the dated Greek papyri from the town thin out after the 640s; the medieval town of el-Bahnasa spoke Coptic and then Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek documents of the Apion estate and the city to the 610s-620s; papyri dated by the Persian occupation (619-629); a few Greek documents of the early Arab period; Coptic then Arabic afterwards. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Occupied by the Persians (619-629); taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the registers were put into Arabic in 705/706 under the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). The Arabic epic of the conquest of el-Bahnasa is legendary.
cities.bilingual_evidence: gymnasium and gymnasial class; boule from 200/201; theatre; thousands of Greek private letters, contracts and literary papyri of residents (Oxyrhynchus Papyri); later the metropolitan see of Arcadia
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Oxyrhynchite nome; gymnasium; boule from 200/201; see with bishops from 325 (Pelagios); Hierocles (Arcadia)
cities.note: The origin of the Arabic name el-Bahnasa is uncertain, so no continuity with the Egyptian or Coptic name is claimed.
sources: Bowman et al., Oxyrhynchus: A City and its Texts (2007)

cities.site: unlocated, Fayum, Faiyum Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Named after Theodosius I or II; first attested in a Greek papyrus of 447 as a city with its own nome in the Fayum.
cities.until_text: Administration: the Theodosiopolite nome was dissolved by the mid or later 7th c. and survived only as a subregion of the Arsinoite into the 8th c. Speech: its people followed the Fayum's shift to Coptic and Arabic in the 7th-8th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek papyri name the city and its nome from 447 (also P.Oxy. LI 3636, 5th c.); the joint pagarchy of Arsinoe and Theodosiopolis last appears in 622 (CPR XIX 32) and the Theodosiopolite nome in 644 (BGU I 320); traces of it as a part of the Arsinoite in the 8th c. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act. The Fayum fell to the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641 (John of Nikiu); the separate nome was merged back into the Arsinoite under Arab rule; the registers were put into Arabic in 705/706 under the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik.
cities.bilingual_evidence: a city (civitas) with its own nome carved from the Arsinoite, attested in Greek papyri from 447; city of Arcadia in Hierocles; its affairs were run by officials of Arsinoe; no bishop of its own is recorded
cities.status_evidence: Hierocles (Arcadia); Greek papyri from 447 (city and nome); no bishop recorded
cities.note: Site unknown: Tebtunis has been proposed but is doubted. A 'formal city' administered from Arsinoe, so a Greek-speaking civic body of its own is not clearly shown.
sources: Tyche: 'The City Solution? Theodosiopolis and the System of Joint Administration in the Late Antique Fayyum'

cities.other_names: Toou (Greek form of the earlier village name)
cities.site: Taha el-Amida (Taha el-Amudein), Minya district, Minya Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Promoted to a city and named after Theodosius I or II, so by 450 at the latest; attested as a city by Hierocles (c. 527).
cities.until_text: Administration: Greek ended in the registers in 705/706 (al-Kindi). Speech: no local Greek evidence after the 6th-7th c.; the area followed the Hermopolite shift to Coptic and then Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: No dated Greek texts of residents are known from the town itself; the Hermopolite as a whole has Greek documents into the 8th c. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and passed to the Arabs with the rest of Upper Egypt under the treaty of Alexandria concluded with 'Amr ibn al-'As (641); the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
cities.pre_greek_note: The city was the former village Toou (Greek spelling); its Egyptian form is not given here because it is not securely attested.
cities.bilingual_evidence: city of the Thebaid in Hierocles; created out of the Hermopolite nome, whose towns have abundant Greek documents
cities.status_evidence: Hierocles (Thebaid); no bishop recorded
cities.note: The Barrington Atlas (75 D4) identifies Theodosiopolis with the village Toou at Taha el-Amida north of Minya; whether the Arabic name continues Toou is not certain. Not to be confused with Theodosiopolis in the Fayum.

cities.site: Qaw el-Kebir (El-Etmaniya), Asyut Governorate (El-Badari district)
cities.greek_from_text: nome metropolis under Rome: the Greek-speaking metropolite and gymnasial class was registered in every metropolis from AD 4/5 (boule from 200/201); no earlier town-specific Greek evidence found; metropolis of the Antaiopolite nome; temple of Antaios built under Ptolemy IV, enlarged under Ptolemy VI and restored under Marcus Aurelius (Greek dedications); see; Hierocles (Ἀνταίου)
cities.until_text: Speech: Greek-writing landowners and officials of the city are attested to the 7th c.; the population spoke Coptic. Administration: the pagarchy of Antaiopolis continued under Arab rule with Greek and Coptic paperwork until Arabic began replacing Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Aphrodito papyri (6th c.) show Antaiopolite notables writing Greek; in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech here: the Greek-speaking community faded by gradual shift to Coptic. Greek administration ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Antaiopolite nome; a see; seat of a boule and later a pagarchy; Greek contracts and petitions of its citizens in the 6th-c. Aphrodito papyri
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Antaiopolite nome; temple of Antaios built under Ptolemy IV, enlarged under Ptolemy VI and restored under Marcus Aurelius (Greek dedications); see; Hierocles (Ἀνταίου)
cities.note: The temple of Antaios, still standing in 1813, was swept away by the Nile in 1821.

cities.site: Kom Ishqaw, Sohag Governorate (Tahta district)
cities.greek_from_text: nome metropolis under Rome: the Greek-speaking metropolite and gymnasial class was registered in every metropolis from AD 4/5 (boule from 200/201); no earlier town-specific Greek evidence found; metropolis of the Aphroditopolite nome (Ptolemy, Geog. 4.5; polis in documents of the 2nd c. BC - 2nd c. AD); a kome from the 3rd c. (Trismegistos Geo 237)
cities.until_text: City status: metropolis in the early Roman period; a village (kome) of the Antaiopolite nome from the 3rd c. on, with autopragia granted under Leo I (457-474). Speech: Dioscorus' circle wrote Greek and Coptic (6th c.); the village archives of the early 8th c. are Coptic for residents' own affairs and Greek and Arabic for the governor's letters (Qurra ibn Sharik, 709-714). Administration: Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
cities.fade_evidence: Dioscorus' Greek poems and contracts (c. 540-585); his own Coptic documents; Basileios archive 709-714: Greek letters of the governor, Coptic for village business; in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech here: the Greek-speaking community faded by gradual shift to Coptic. Greek administration ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). The village came under the Arab pagarchy of Ishqaw in the early 8th c.
cities.pre_greek_note: Per-Wadjet is given for Aphroditopolis of the 10th Upper Egyptian nome in standard lists; the identification with Kom Ishqaw is the usual one but not beyond doubt.
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Aphroditopolite nome in the early Roman period; later a large village whose landowners wrote Greek: Dioscorus of Aphrodito (c. 520-585), notary and Greek poet; Greek and Coptic archive of the pagarch Basileios (709-714)
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Aphroditopolite nome (Ptolemy, Geog. 4.5; polis in documents of the 2nd c. BC - 2nd c. AD); a kome from the 3rd c. (Trismegistos Geo 237)
cities.note: Counted for its metropolis phase; in the 6th c. (its best-documented period) it was legally a village, though larger than many cities.
sources: Fournet (ed.), Les archives de Dioscore d'Aphrodité (2008)

cities.site: Kom Isfaht, Asyut Governorate (Abu Tig district)
cities.greek_from_text: metropolis of a separate nome by the early 2nd c. AD (archive of the strategos Apollonios, 113-120)
cities.until_text: Speech: Greek-speaking metropolite class of the Roman period; shift to Coptic in the 6th-7th c. In the early Islamic period the district became the kura of Qahqawa. Administration: the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Few documents from the town itself after the 2nd c.; in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech here: the Greek-speaking community faded by gradual shift to Coptic. Greek administration ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
cities.pre_greek_note: The Coptic name Sbeht (continued in Arabic Isfaht) is not Greek; its Egyptian original is not securely identified.
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Apollonopolite Heptakomias nome; Greek archive of the strategos Apollonios and his family (113-120); a city in Hierocles (Ἀπόλλωνος)
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Apollonopolite Heptakomias nome (Apollonios archive, P.Giss., P.Brem.); Hierocles
cities.note: Keep apart from Apollonopolis Mikra/Parva (Qus) and Apollonopolis Magna (Edfu). The Apollonios archive shows a strategos from Hermopolis, an official; the resident Greek-speaking class is inferred from metropolis status.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: Edfu, Aswan Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek ostraca and papyri of residents from the Ptolemaic period (Tell Edfu excavations)
cities.until_text: Speech: Greek-speaking settlers, Jews and civic class from the Ptolemaic period; shift to Coptic in the 6th-7th c.; Edfu's medieval documents are Coptic and Arabic. Administration: the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek ostraca of Edfu to the 7th c.; Coptic papyri from Edfu (7th-11th c.); in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Work on the temple was halted when the rebels of the great Theban revolt held the region (206-186 BC; Edfu building inscription). Greek administration ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Apollonopolite nome; Greek and Demotic ostraca of residents from the Ptolemaic period (Tell Edfu); a Jewish community with Greek names (Greek tax receipts, 1st c. AD); a see
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Apollonopolite nome; see; Hierocles (Ἀπόλλωνος)

cities.other_names: Apollonopolis Mikra; Diocletianopolis (c. 300); Kōs Berbir (Coptic); Qus (Arabic)
cities.site: Qus, Qena Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: raised to a city as Diocletianopolis under the tetrarchs, c. 300 (first attestation as a city)
cities.until_text: Speech: Greek-speaking civic and clerical class of the late Roman city; shift to Coptic in the 6th-7th c.; medieval Qus became the chief Muslim city of Upper Egypt. Administration: the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: In the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech here: the Greek-speaking community faded by gradual shift to Coptic. Greek administration ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
cities.bilingual_evidence: a city as Diocletianopolis in Hierocles and Georgius Cyprius (if the identification holds) and a see; Greek name of the town
cities.status_evidence: Hierocles 732.3 and Georgius Cyprius 772 (Διοκλητιανούπολις); see (bishop of Apollonopolis Parva at Ephesus, 431?)
cities.note: Not a nome metropolis; the identification of Diocletianopolis with Qus (Gelzer) is probable but not certain, and Greek-speaking residents are inferred from city and see status. Keep apart from Apollonopolis Heptakomias (Kom Isfaht) and Apollonopolis Magna (Edfu).
sources: Timm, Das christlich-koptische Ägypten, s.v. Qus

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: Qift, Qena Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek traders and settlers at the Nile end of the Red Sea roads opened by Ptolemy II; Greek dedications at Koptos from the Ptolemaic period

cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek settlers at Syene and Elephantine from the early Ptolemaic period (P.Eleph. 1, 311 BC); Greek ostraca of residents (Ptolemaic and Roman); a see from the 4th c.; Greek family archive of Patermouthis, soldier and boatman of Syene and Elephantine (493-613)
cities.status_evidence: see from the 4th c. (Bishop Appion of Syene, 425-450); Syene in Strabo and Ptolemy; Greek documents of residents
cities.note: Syene was always a garrison town; it counts here for its Greek settler families, its see and the Patermouthis documents. The fort island of Elephantine opposite is treated with Syene.
sources: Farber & Porten, The Patermouthis Archive (in The Elephantine Papyri in English, 1996)

cities.site: Dendera, Qena Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek dedication of the Isis propylon by 'those from the metropolis and the nome', year 31 of Augustus, AD 1/2 (OGIS 659; first attestation of the civic body); an earlier Greek dedication by the local strategos Ptolemaios son of Panas, 12 BC
cities.until_text: Speech: Greek-speaking metropolite class of the Roman period; shift to Coptic in the 6th-7th c. Administration: the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Pachomian sources (4th c.) show the bishop of Tentyra among Coptic-speaking monks; in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech here: the Greek-speaking community faded by gradual shift to Coptic. Greek administration ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
cities.bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Tentyrite nome; Greek dedications of temple buildings by 'those from the metropolis and the nome' (propylon of the Isis temple, AD 1; pronaos of the Hathor temple, AD 35/36); see (Sarapion of Tentyra, 4th c.)
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Tentyrite nome; Greek civic dedications (AD 1, AD 35/36); Juvenal 15 on the feud of Tentyra and Ombos (AD 127); see; Hierocles (Τέντυρα)

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.other_names: Diospolis Megale; Djeme (Coptic, the west-bank town); Luxor (Arabic al-Uqsur)
cities.site: Luxor (Karnak and Luxor temples, east bank), Luxor Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek residents and Greek documents at Thebes from the 3rd c. BC
cities.until_text: Speech: a Greek-speaking minority from the 3rd c. BC; Thebes was reduced to a group of villages after 88 BC (Strabo 17.1.46) but Greek ostraca of residents continue through the Roman period; in the 6th-8th c. the Theban towns (Djeme) used Coptic for their own contracts and letters, with Greek formulae and protocols. Administration: the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Thousands of Greek ostraca from Thebes (Ptolemaic to 7th c.); the Coptic legal documents of Djeme (7th-8th c.); in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Acts against the city: held by the rebel pharaohs Haronnophris and Chaonnophris in the great Theban revolt (206-186 BC); sacked by Ptolemy IX Soter II after the revolt of 88-86 BC (Pausanias 1.9.3); taken by C. Cornelius Gallus in the revolt of 29 BC (Philae stele); legionary fortress built in the Luxor temple under Diocletian (c. 300); the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
cities.bilingual_evidence: Greek residents from the 3rd c. BC (Greek tax receipts and bank documents; the lawsuit of the Greek officer Hermias over a house in Thebes, 117 BC); metropolis of the Theban nome with its gymnasial class in the Roman period
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Theban nome (Diospolis Magna); Greek documents of residents
cities.note: Arabic al-Uqsur ('the castles') refers to the Roman fortress and temples, not to an ancient name of the city. Strabo already describes Thebes as villages, but the Greek-writing community did not disappear.
sources: Philae stele of Cornelius Gallus (29 BC)

cities.list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.other_names: Kleopatris (Strabo 17.1.25-26); Klysma (Roman and later; Hierocles); Peklousma (Coptic); al-Qulzum (Arabic, after the conquest; hence Bahr al-Qulzum, the Arabic name of the Red Sea)
cities.site: Kom el-Qolzum (Tell el-Qulzum), north side of Suez, Suez Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: founded by Ptolemy II at the head of the Gulf of Suez, at the end of his Nile-Red Sea canal, and named after his sister-wife Arsinoe II, c. 270 BC (Strabo 17.1.25-26; the Pithom stele records a foundation named Arsinoe, which may be this one); later renamed Kleopatris; rebuilt as Klysma under Trajan, early 2nd c. AD
cities.until_text: Klysma was a Greek-speaking port town and bishop's see into the 6th c. (bishops to 553; pilgrims describe its port and church c. 570). Administration: taken with Egypt by the Arabs in 641; 'Amr ibn al-'As reopened the canal to the port, now al-Qulzum, to ship Egyptian grain to Arabia; Greek orders of the governor Qurra ibn Sharik (708-710) name it only as the base of the Arab fleet. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: bishops Iakob (before 347), Tithoes and Paulos (347), Poimen (458/459) and Stephanos (Council of Constantinople, 553) (Worp 1994); Egeria (c. 383/384) and the Piacenza pilgrim (c. 570) describe the port and its church; after the conquest Klysma appears in Greek papyri only as the base of the Arab fleet, in orders of the governor Qurra ibn Sharik to Aphrodito (P. Lond. IV 1346 and 1383, 708-710), which are administrative Greek, not evidence of Greek speakers at Klysma. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: Taken with the rest of Egypt by the Arabs under 'Amr ibn al-'As, 641; under the caliphs the port became al-Qulzum. No named act ended Greek speech there. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.status_evidence: royal foundation of Ptolemy II (Pithom stele; Strabo 17.1.25-26); Klysma a bishop's see 347-553 (Worp, ZPE 100, 1994); Klysma listed by Hierocles (as a kastron)
cities.note: The Ptolemaic town and Roman Klysma are usually placed at or near Kom el-Qolzum on the north side of Suez; some scholars put Arsinoe a few km away. Treated as one place; the mound is now largely built over.
cities.refoundations: Arsinoe -> Kleopatris (renamed under a Cleopatra, same place) -> Klysma (rebuilt by Trajan, early 2nd c. AD; same area)

cities.list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.other_names: Berenike Trogodytike; Berenike (Strabo, Pliny); the nearby modern town Berenice (Baranis) takes its name from it
cities.site: Medinet el-Haras, south of the town of Berenice (Baranis), Red Sea Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: founded by Ptolemy II and named after his mother Berenike I (Pliny NH 6.168; Strabo 17.1.45), c. 275 BC; the earliest excavated levels are of the 3rd c. BC
cities.until_text: The port shrank in the late 3rd c., revived in the 4th-5th c. and was abandoned some time before the mid-6th c.; the last shrine went out of use by the early 6th c. The bay later silted up and the site was never reoccupied.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek ostraca and papyri of the 1st c. AD (O. Berenike I-III) beside Latin, Tamil-Brahmi, Prakrit, Hebrew, Palmyrene and South Arabian texts; late Roman church; Greek inscriptions of Blemmyan kings (late 4th-5th c.); pottery of the last phase runs to the early 6th c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: abandoned before the mid-6th c., after a last phase under Blemmyan kings (Isemne, Kabantia); the excavators point to the collapse of the Red Sea trade. No destruction is recorded.
cities.other_language: Blemmyan (in the last phase, late 4th to early 6th c.), beside Egyptian
cities.bilingual_evidence: in the last phase the town had a Blemmyan population and was apparently ruled by Blemmyan kings: Greek inscriptions of the late 4th-5th c. name the kings Isemne and Kabantia, and the late Falcon Shrine served Blemmyan worshippers (Oller Guzman et al., AJA 126, 2022); Greek remained the written language
cities.status_evidence: royal foundation of Ptolemy II (Pliny NH 6.168); seat of the praefectus montis Berenicidis in the Roman period; Greek ostraca and papyri of residents; excavations 1994-2001 and from 2008
cities.note: A multilingual port town (Greek, Egyptian, Latin, Indian, South Arabian and Aksumite visitors and residents); Greek was the main language of its documents. How far the Blemmyes controlled the last town is debated.
sources: Sidebotham, Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route (2011)

cities.list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
cities.other_names: 'the city of Oasis' (Hdt. 3.26); Hibiton polis ('city of the Hibites'); Ibis; Hebet (Egyptian); metropolis of the Great Oasis (Oasis Magna); the town site is now called Ain Turba (Arabic)
cities.site: Ain Turba and the Temple of Hibis, with the Bagawat necropolis to the north, 2-3 km north of El-Kharga, New Valley Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek-writing civic elite first clearly attested c. 300: the wealthy Hellenized households of Ain Turba (late 3rd-early 4th c., with an Iliad school tablet) and the councillors of the 4th c. Hibis had long been the seat of the administration of the Great Oasis (prefects' edicts of AD 49 and 68 published at its temple), but that is official Greek. Herodotus (3.26) says that in 525 BC 'the city of Oasis' was held by Samians 'said to be of the Aeschrionian tribe'; this single report is not counted as the start of a Greek city.
cities.until_text: Administration: the oasis passed under Arab rule after the conquest of Egypt (641); Greek stayed in the government of Egypt until 706. Speech: Greek graffiti at Bagawat still name the 'polis of Hibis' in the 7th-8th c.; a Coptic graffito of 784-883 at Gebel el-Teir shows the town still existed, by then writing Coptic. Greek gave way to Coptic and then Arabic.
cities.fade_evidence: 4th-c. Greek and Coptic ostraca and an Iliad school tablet from the Ain Turba houses (Bagnall & Tallet 2015); Greek graffiti at Bagawat of the 7th-8th c.; Coptic graffito of 784-883 at Gebel el-Teir
cities.ended_by: No named act ended Greek: the Blemmyes raided the Oasis c. 440-450 and carried off the exiled Nestorius (Nestorius' letters in Evagrius, HE 1.7), and the nearby monastery of Deir el-Bagawat was given up in the mid-5th c., possibly after such raids, but the town survived; after the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (641/642) Greek faded as Coptic and then Arabic took over.
cities.bilingual_evidence: administrative centre of the Great Oasis; probable councillors (bouleutai) in the 4th-c. Douch ostraca; a polis in P. Lips. I 64 (368/9); houses of a Hellenized elite at Ain Turba (late 3rd-4th c.) with Greek ostraca and a school tablet with Iliad phrases beside Coptic letters; Greek graffiti at Bagawat naming the 'polis of Hibis' (7th-8th c.)
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Great Oasis; bouleutai late 3rd-4th c. (Douch ostraca, as interpreted by Bagnall & Tallet 2015); polis in P. Lips. I 64 (368/9); see of the Great Oasis (Oasis Magna) in Thebaid I in the later lists of sees
cities.note: The Samians of Hdt. 3.26 are often taken as Greek traders settled in the oasis under Amasis; nothing else is known of them. Bagnall and Tallet (2019) stress how little is known of the administration of the oasis. The ancient town lies largely under fields. The Demotic ostraca of the Persian period from Ayn Manawir in the same oasis (5th-4th c. BC; Chauveau) show an Egyptian-speaking farming community and no Greek settlers, which supports not opening a Greek phase in 525 BC.
sources: Bagnall & Tallet (eds.), The Great Oasis of Egypt (2019)

cities.list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
cities.other_names: Mothiton polis ('city of the Mothites'); Mathon
cities.site: Mut el-Kharab, on the edge of Mut, Dakhla Oasis, New Valley Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: 'the city of the Mothites' in Greek contracts from Kellis of c. 299 (SB XXIV 15901, restored) and 320 (P. Kell. I Gr. 52); capital of the Mothite nome, probably created about then; listed as a polis beside Hibis and Trimithis in P. Lips. I 64 (368/9)
cities.until_text: Pottery and a church show the town in use to the 6th-7th c. and later (Fatimid and Mamluk pottery). No Greek texts of residents later than the 4th-5th c. have been published, but documentation from the oasis is thin after c. 400, so the silence is not evidence of an early end. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: 4th-c. Greek and Coptic papyri of the Mothite nome (Kellis); church and pottery to the 6th-7th c. (Dakhleh Oasis Project). Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town lived on, and Greek gave way to Coptic and then Arabic after the Arab conquest of Egypt (641). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.pre_greek_note: The Dakhleh Oasis Project gives the Egyptian name as Mt/Mrt; Trismegistos and the 4CARE gazetteer give Pa-Mwt (with a query in Trismegistos).
cities.bilingual_evidence: capital of the Mothite nome and a polis from c. 299 (Kellis contracts; P. Lips. I 64, 368/9); seat of a bishop in the 4th c.; Greek and Coptic documents from the nome (Kellis papyri) show a Greek-writing local elite tied to the city
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Mothite nome; polis in SB XXIV 15901 (c. 299), P. Kell. I Gr. 52 (320) and P. Lips. I 64 (368/9); bishop's seat in the 4th c.; Trismegistos Places 3154
cities.note: Most Greek evidence for the Mothite nome comes from the village of Kellis; the city itself is little excavated, and the date of the Mothite nome is not certain (Bagnall and Tallet 2019 warn that the administration of the oasis is poorly known).
sources: Bagnall & Tallet (eds.), The Great Oasis of Egypt (2019)

cities.list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.other_names: Mus Hormos; the site was reoccupied as the medieval port of Quseir al-Qadim (Arabic)
cities.site: Quseir al-Qadim, 8 km north of El-Quseir, Red Sea Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Ptolemaic harbour, first named by Agatharchides (mid-2nd c. BC; Diod. 3.39); a foundation under Ptolemy II is often assumed, but the excavations found little Ptolemaic material; the Roman port town flourished from the late 1st c. BC
cities.until_text: The Roman harbour silted and the town was given up; the excavators date the end of Roman occupation to the 3rd c., with the harbour largely disused by the mid-2nd c. The site was reoccupied only as the Islamic port of Quseir al-Qadim (12th-15th c.).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek ostraca and papyri of the 1st-2nd c. AD (letters, accounts, customs passes) beside Latin, South Arabian, Tamil and Nabataean texts; no Roman occupation layers after the 3rd c.
cities.ended_by: No named act: abandoned as the harbour silted and the trade moved to Berenike and Klysma (excavators' view).
cities.status_evidence: Ptolemaic and Roman port town (Strabo 16.4.24, 17.1.45; Periplus 1, 19); identified by Peacock and Blue's excavations; Greek ostraca and papyri of residents; no civic institutions attested
cities.note: A port town of traders, soldiers and officials with no attested civic institutions; included as a Ptolemaic port settlement with Greek-speaking residents, as Cohen and Mueller treat it.
sources: Peacock & Blue, Myos Hormos - Quseir al-Qadim (2006, 2011)

cities.list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: unlocated; Red Sea coast between the Gulf of Suez and Quseir (Mersa Gawasis and the Safaga area have been proposed), Red Sea Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: founded under Ptolemy II by his officer Satyros and named after the king's sister Philotera, c. 270 BC (Strabo 16.4.5, after Artemidorus; Pithom stele)
cities.until_text: Nothing is known of the town after its foundation; Strabo's source (c. 100 BC) still names it and Ptolemy's Geography (mid-2nd c. AD) lists only a harbour of that name. No remains have been identified.
cities.fade_evidence: last named by Ptolemy, Geog. 4.5 (mid-2nd c. AD), as a harbour
cities.ended_by: No named act: the place is unlocated and simply drops out of the sources.
cities.status_evidence: royal foundation of Ptolemy II (Strabo 16.4.5); Cohen 2006 (Red Sea foundations)
cities.note: Included as a named royal foundation; no town remains or Greek documents of residents are known, and it may never have been more than a harbour settlement.

cities.list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
cities.other_names: chief place of the Small Oasis (Oasis Parva); the oasis was later called the 'Oasis of Oxyrhynchus' (Coptic period) and the 'Oasis of el-Bahnasa' (Arabic)
cities.site: El-Qasr, beside El-Bawiti, Bahariya Oasis, Giza Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Greek dedications from the town, c. AD 1 (SB XXII 15621; SEG LIII 1956); earlier Greek presence in the oasis (Alexander's temple of Ammon at Qasr el-Miqisba; Greco-Roman necropolis at El-Bawiti) does not show a civic community
cities.until_text: Greek ostraca of the oasis run to the early 5th c., a pagarch is attested in the 5th-6th c., and 5th-c. churches carry Greek inscriptions; the later oasis was Coptic-speaking ('Oasis of Oxyrhynchus') and then Arabic. Later Greek evidence is lacking, but so is evidence of any kind. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
cities.fade_evidence: Greek ostraca dated 374/5-412/3 (era years); Bir Shawish ostraca to 403 and the 5th c.; 5th-c. churches with Greek inscriptions (found 2019-2021). Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
cities.ended_by: No named act: Greek faded in late antiquity and after the Arab conquest of Egypt (641); the oasis later became Muslim. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
cities.pre_greek_note: Egyptian form as given by Trismegistos (with the gloss 'the wall'); no hieroglyphic or Demotic attestation is cited.
