cities.bilingual_evidence: called the metropolis of the Small Oasis (Wagner 1987; Trismegistos); Greek dedications from the town of the 1st c. AD (SB XXII 15621; SEG LIII 1956); Greek ostraca of the oasis, 374/5-412/3; 5th-c. churches with Greek inscriptions
cities.status_evidence: metropolis of the Small Oasis according to Wagner 1987 and Trismegistos Places 8248; Greek dedications of the 1st c. AD; no boule, gymnasium or bishop known
cities.note: The Small Oasis was closely tied to the Oxyrhynchite nome, and its civic status is poorly documented; included only on the evidence that Psobthis was the metropolis of the oasis.

cities.list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
cities.site: Amheida, Dakhla Oasis, New Valley Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: a village that became a polis by 304, when a Greek contract from Kellis names a man 'from the city of the Trimithites' (P. Kell. I Gr. 49); the date of the grant is unknown. The house of the councillor Serenos (c. 340-365), the Greek school and P. Lips. I 64 (368/9) show the city in the mid-4th c.
cities.until_text: The town declined after the 360s (the house of Serenos abandoned c. 365); coins run to the end of the 4th or the early 5th c., when dunes covered the town. It was never reoccupied.
cities.fade_evidence: house B1 (Serenos) abandoned c. 365; coins to the late 4th/early 5th c.; sand invasion at the end of the 4th c. or soon after (Davoli in An Oasis City, 2015)
cities.ended_by: No named act: decline after the 360s and abandonment around 400, as dunes invaded the town and the water supply failed (excavators' view).
cities.bilingual_evidence: a polis by 304 (P. Kell. I Gr. 49) and beside Hibis and Mothis in P. Lips. I 64 (368/9); house of the city councillor Serenos with household records in Greek; a school (mid-4th c.) with Greek verses painted on the walls; Greek ostraca of residents (O. Trim.)
cities.status_evidence: polis in P. Kell. I Gr. 49 (304) and P. Lips. I 64 (368/9); councillor Serenos (O. Trim.); NYU excavations from 2004
cities.note: Kellis, 30 km to the east, has richer Greek papyri but remained a village.
sources: Bagnall et al., An Oasis City (2015)

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.other_names: Leukaspis (Λευκάσπις)? (both names are proposed for the excavated town)
cities.site: Marina El Alamein, Matrouh Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: the excavated town at Marina el-Alamein was founded in the second half of the 2nd c. BC (Polish excavations)
cities.until_text: The town declined after an earthquake in the mid-3rd c. AD and was abandoned at the end of the 6th or beginning of the 7th c.; Greek speech ended with the abandonment.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek public inscriptions for Trajan or Hadrian, for the prefect of Egypt T. Flavius Titianus (129) and for Commodus (182-183); church of c. 400; bishops of Antiphrai Menas (362) and Apollo (458/459); desertion c. 600.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the town shrank after the mid-3rd-c. earthquake (natural) and was deserted c. 600, before the Arab conquest of 642.
cities.status_evidence: forum/agora, civic basilica, baths and Greek public inscriptions; see of Antiphrai (bishops 362, 458/459), if the identification holds
cities.note: The ancient name of the Marina el-Alamein town is not secure (Antiphrai or Leukaspis). The site lies at the western edge of the Mareotis and may also appear among the Egyptian cities.

cities.site: Tobruk, Butnan District
cities.greek_from_text: first named as a harbour of Marmarica in Roman-period sources (Ptolemy; Stadiasmus Maris Magni); a see in late antiquity
cities.until_text: Administration: a harbour town and see of Libya Inferior until 'Amr ibn al-'As's advance through Marmarica, 642. Speech: Greek after the conquest is not attested. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed: no Greek text of a resident is known from after 642, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest of Barqa name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam). The end date is that of the conquest, and the range allows for a remnant.
cities.fade_evidence: bishop Serapion at Nicaea, 325; Aemilianus at the council of Constantinople, 553; Justinian made it a garrisoned stronghold against the Moors (Procopius, Buildings 6.2.2); no later Greek evidence.
cities.ended_by: Arab conquest of Marmarica by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642; no named later act.
cities.status_evidence: Greek name; harbour town; see of Libya Inferior (Serapion at Nicaea 325; Aemilianus 553); stronghold under Justinian
cities.note: Positive evidence of a resident Greek-speaking civic community is thin: a Greek name, a harbour and a see in a province whose hinterland was Libyan.

cities.site: Susa (Marsa Susa), Jabal al Akhdar District
cities.greek_from_text: harbour of Cyrene from its early years (earliest finds c. 600 BC); an independent city of the Pentapolis from the Hellenistic period (2nd-1st c. BC)
cities.until_text: Administration: seat of the governor of Libya Superior in the 6th c.; Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: Greek after 643 is not attested; the town seems to have shrunk to little after the conquest. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
cities.fade_evidence: damage in the earthquake of 365 and subsidence of the harbour (natural); 5th-6th c. churches and the governor's palace with Greek inscriptions; no Greek text after 643. The modern town was founded in 1897 by Muslim refugees from Crete, many Greek-speaking: later newcomers, not a continuation of the ancient community.
cities.ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri); no named later act. Earlier: the earthquake of 365 (natural) and the raids of Synesius' time.
cities.status_evidence: Pentapolis city (Strabo 17.3.20 as harbour of Cyrene; independent city from the Hellenistic period); renamed Sozousa and seat of the governor of Libya Superior; see in late antiquity
cities.note: The move of the governor's seat from Ptolemais is dated to the 5th or 6th c.; one recent study puts it c. 468-470.
cities.refoundations: Renamed Sozousa in late antiquity (same site)

cities.site: Wadi el-Khalij, near Bomba on the Gulf of Bomba, Derna District
cities.greek_from_text: the Theraean colonists moved from Platea to Aziris and stayed six years before moving to Cyrene in 631 BC (Hdt. 4.157-158); Greek pottery from c. 640 BC at the site
cities.until_text: Herodotus has the colonists leave for Cyrene after six years; the excavated pottery runs to c. 570 BC, so a small Greek settlement stayed on until then.
cities.fade_evidence: excavated pottery from c. 640 to c. 570 BC.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the colonists moved to Cyrene, guided by Libyans, c. 631 BC (Hdt. 4.158); the remaining settlement was given up c. 570 BC.
cities.status_evidence: seat of the Theraean colony for six years (Hdt. 4.157-158); excavated Greek settlement
cities.note: It housed the whole colonial community before Cyrene, but it was a temporary seat rather than a lasting city.

cities.other_names: Barqa (Arabic; capital of the Arab province, whose name passed to all Cyrenaica)
cities.site: old town of Al Marj (destroyed by the 1963 earthquake), Marj District
cities.greek_from_text: founded c. 560-550 BC by brothers of King Arkesilaos II of Cyrene who quarrelled with him (Hdt. 4.160)
cities.until_text: Administration: Barke capitulated to 'Amr ibn al-'As in 642/643 and became Barqa, capital of the Arab province. Speech: Greek after 643 is not attested; Arab writers describe its people as Berbers (Lawata) and Arabs. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
cities.fade_evidence: sacked by the Persians, 515/514 BC; eclipsed by its harbour Ptolemais from the 3rd c. BC and a small town under Rome; bishops Zopyros (325), Zenobios (431), Theodoros (449); al-Bakri (11th c.) describes Barqa as a prosperous Muslim town exporting wool and honey; decline after the Banu Hilal invasion (11th c.).
cities.ended_by: Capitulated to 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643, agreeing a tribute of 13,000 dinars (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri). Earlier: besieged and sacked by the Persian satrap Aryandes for Pheretime, 515/514 BC, part of its people deported to Bactria by Darius I (Hdt. 4.200-204). No named act ends Greek speech after 643. Later: c. 688-690 an imperial force landed in Cyrenaica and killed the Arab commander Zuhayr ibn Qays al-Balawi near Barqa, and Barqa was briefly out of Muslim control; no Greek-speaking civil community is attested in connection with it.
cities.founder: brothers of Arkesilaos II of Cyrene
cities.pre_greek_note: Herodotus says the founders won over the local Libyans (4.160); no earlier town is known at the site.
cities.status_evidence: IACP 1025; coinage of the 5th-4th c. BC; see (bishops at Nicaea 325, Ephesus 431 and 449)
cities.note: Barke lay inland; its harbour became Ptolemais (separate entry). No ancient remains are visible at Al Marj.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: Sidi Khrebish, Benghazi, Benghazi District
cities.greek_from_text: founded c. 250-246 BC beside Euesperides and named after Berenike II, daughter of Magas and wife of Ptolemy III
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: the Sidi Khrebish quarter was occupied into the 7th c.; Greek after 643 is not attested. Medieval Barniq was a small place; the modern name Benghazi comes from a local saint. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
cities.fade_evidence: Greek decrees of the Jewish politeuma (1st c. BC-1st c. AD); bishop Dachius at Nicaea, 325; Justinian rebuilt the circuit wall and built a public bath (Procopius, Buildings 6.2.5); no Greek text after 643.
cities.ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri); no named later act.
cities.founder: a Ptolemaic ruler, traditionally Ptolemy III (named for Berenike II)
cities.status_evidence: Pentapolis city; Greek civic and Jewish politeuma decrees; see (Dachius at Nicaea 325)
cities.note: The founder is disputed: some credit Berenike II herself, in the years after Magas' death, rather than Ptolemy III.
sources: Lloyd (ed.), Excavations at Sidi Khrebish, Benghazi (Berenice)

cities.other_names: Claudiopolis (briefly, after the earthquake of 262, honouring Claudius II); Grennah (local Arabic form recorded by 19th-c. travellers); Qurina (modern Arabic name of the ruins)
cities.site: Shahhat, Jabal al Akhdar District
cities.greek_from_text: founded by Theraean colonists under Battos I (Aristoteles), 631 BC by the traditional date (Hdt. 4.150-159; Pindar, Pythian 4-5); the earliest Greek pottery at the site is of the late 7th c. BC
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest of the Pentapolis, 642/643. Speech: Greek was the language of the shrunken late-antique town (Greek inscriptions of the 5th-6th c.); no Greek text of residents after 643 is known, and how long a Greek-speaking remnant stayed is unknown. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
cities.fade_evidence: Jewish revolt of 115-117: temples of Apollo and Zeus, the Caesareum and roads destroyed (Dio 68.32; Euseb. HE 4.2), rebuilt under Hadrian; earthquake of 262 and the great earthquake of 21 July 365 (natural); seat of government moved to Ptolemais c. 300; Synesius (c. 400-413) describes a poor, half-empty city and raids by the Ausurians (Austuriani) in 405 and 411-412; the inhabited area shrank in the 5th-6th c., but the Central and East churches were built then and bishops are known to Leontius (c. 600); no Greek text after 643.
cities.ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri). Earlier blows: the Jewish revolt of 115-117 under Lukuas (Andreas), the Marmaritae raid repulsed in 268/269, the raids of the Ausurians (Austuriani) and Macetae described by Synesius (405, 411-412), and the earthquakes of 262 and 365 (natural events). No named act ends Greek speech after 643.
cities.pre_greek_note: Herodotus says Libyans led the settlers to the spring of Apollo (4.158); no pre-Greek town is known at the site.
cities.status_evidence: IACP 1028; civic coinage from the 6th c. BC; boule, demos, gymnasium and ephebes; Pentapolis city; see in late antiquity
cities.note: The colonists' earlier seats at Platea and Aziris are separate entries.
cities.refoundations: Restored by Hadrian after the revolt of 115-117 (same site); briefly Claudiopolis after 262

cities.site: Derna, Derna District
cities.greek_from_text: first named in Roman-period geography (Ptolemy, 2nd c. AD) as a town at the eastern edge of the Pentapolis; a Greek see by the 4th c.
cities.until_text: Administration: civil and later church metropolis of Libya Inferior; Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: Greek after the conquest is not attested. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
cities.fade_evidence: bishops Piso (347), Dioscurus (c. 410, in a dispute with Paul of Erythron settled by Synesius, Ep. 67), Daniel (431), Theodore (5th c., John Moschus); no Greek evidence after 643.
cities.ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri); no named later act. Later: in 688 raiders from the imperial forces killed the Arab commander Zuhayr ibn Qays al-Balawi and some seventy of his men in the province of Barqa; he is buried at Derna (the Sahaba mosque). This was a military raid and brought back no Greek-speaking community.
cities.pre_greek_note: The name Darnis is not Greek and may be Libyan, but it is known only from Greek and Latin sources.
cities.status_evidence: see from the 4th c. (Piso 347; Daniel at Ephesus 431); metropolis of Libya Inferior
cities.note: Its Greek character rests on the see, Synesius' letters and its place on the Pentapolis coast; its Hellenistic history is unknown. Ptolemy and Ammianus place it in the Pentapolis, later lists in Libya Inferior.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: Al Athrun (Latrun), 9 km east of Ras al-Hilal, Derna District
cities.greek_from_text: a Hellenistic foundation on the coast east of Apollonia: occupation from the 4th c. BC (French excavations); named by Ptolemy (Geography 4.4.3); a see from the second half of the 4th c. AD
cities.until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: the town was occupied until the 8th c., but Greek after 643 is not attested. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
cities.fade_evidence: see from the later 4th c.; bishop Paul (c. 410, Synesius, Ep. 67); a cathedral with baptistery and a pilgrimage church of the 6th c.; occupation to the 8th c.; no Greek text after 643.
cities.ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri); no named later act.
cities.status_evidence: see from the later 4th c. (Paul, c. 410: Synesius, Ep. 67); greatest extent in late antiquity; 6th-c. cathedral and pilgrimage church
cities.note: A village or large town under the early Empire; its rise to a city came with the see. Synesius shows its diocese reaching over the villages of Hydrax and Palaebisca.

cities.site: Sidi Abeid, Benghazi, Benghazi District
cities.greek_from_text: the earliest Greek pottery from the Sidi Abeid excavations is usually put in the early 6th c. BC, though its dating is disputed; Herodotus names the city in the events of 515 BC (4.171, 4.204)
cities.until_text: Abandoned c. 250 BC when its people moved to the new city of Berenike nearby (latest coins of the 250s BC); Greek speech went on at Berenike.
cities.fade_evidence: new settlers sent by Arkesilaos IV c. 462 BC; besieged by Libyans and relieved by Gylippos' Peloponnesian ships in 413 BC (Thuc. 7.50.2); last coins c. 250 BC.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the city was given up c. 250 BC and its people moved to Berenike, named after Berenike II; silting of the harbour lagoon and Ptolemaic policy after the reconquest of Cyrenaica are the usual explanations.
cities.status_evidence: IACP 1026; coinage of the 5th-4th c. BC; Thuc. 7.50.2; Hdt. 4.171, 4.204
cities.note: Euesperides and Berenike are separate sites within Benghazi; the mother city is not recorded and Cyrene is assumed. Some accounts date the foundation as late as c. 525 BC; the city is certainly older than 515 BC.
sources: Wilson et al., Libyan Studies (Euesperides reports)
cities.refoundations: Euesperides -> Berenike (c. 250-246 BC; new site, separate entry)

cities.site: Daryanah (Driana), Benghazi District
cities.greek_from_text: founded by Hadrian (117-138), probably soon after the Jewish revolt, when he sent settlers to the devastated province (Orosius 7.12.6)
cities.until_text: Named in the Antonine Itinerary, the Peutinger Table and the Ravenna Cosmography; its later history and the date it was deserted are unknown.
cities.fade_evidence: no inscriptions, bishops or late-antique texts of the town are known.
cities.ended_by: No named act is recorded for the town; the Pentapolis fell to 'Amr ibn al-'As in 642/643.
cities.status_evidence: imperial foundation bearing Hadrian's name, on the Peutinger Table (with town vignette) and in the Antonine Itinerary
cities.note: The settlers' origin and language are not recorded; Greek is assumed from the Pentapolis setting without direct evidence from the site, which may lie at Wadi Jawbiyah rather than Daryanah.

cities.site: Qasr Libya, between Al Marj and Al Bayda, Jabal al Akhdar District
cities.greek_from_text: named in Roman-period geography (Ptolemy); a see by c. 410 (Synesius)
cities.until_text: Administration: refounded by Justinian as Theodorias in 539; Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: Greek after 643 is not attested. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
cities.fade_evidence: bishops Athamas and Antonios (Synesius, c. 412), Publius (431), Makarios and Theodoros (539/540); Greek mosaic inscriptions of the East Church dated 539/540; no Greek text after 643.
cities.ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri). Earlier: damage from raiders in the 5th and early 6th c. before Justinian's refoundation.
cities.status_evidence: see from c. 410 (Synesius); refounded as a 'new city' (polis nea) Theodorias by Justinian, 539 (dated mosaics)
cities.note: The identification of Qasr Libya with Olbia rests on the mosaics and the episcopal list.

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.site: Marsa Matruh, Matrouh Governorate
cities.greek_from_text: Alexander passed it on his way to Siwa in 331 BC (Arrian, Anabasis 3.3.3); a Ptolemaic harbour and naval base from the 3rd c. BC
cities.until_text: Administration: metropolis of Libya Inferior; taken in 'Amr ibn al-'As's advance west in 642; al-Baratun was then a station on the Arab coastal road. Speech: Greek after the conquest is not attested.
cities.fade_evidence: bishops Titus (Nicaea 325) and Gaius (Alexandria 362); Justinian made it a garrisoned stronghold against the Moors (Procopius, Buildings 6.2.2); no Greek document of residents after 642.
cities.ended_by: Taken by 'Amr ibn al-'As on his march to Barqa, 642; no named later act. Earlier: Cornelius Gallus seized the town for Octavian and beat off Antony's attack, 30 BC (Dio 51.9), without ending it.
cities.pre_greek_note: A Late Bronze Age trading post on Bates's Island in the lagoon (14th-13th c. BC) had Cypriot and Aegean pottery but was not a Greek settlement and has no link with the later town.
cities.status_evidence: Strabo 17.1.14 (city and large harbour); see (Titus at Nicaea 325); metropolis of Libya Inferior; Justinian's stronghold
cities.note: No ancient source records a royal foundation; a foundation by Alexander or the first Ptolemies is sometimes suggested.

cities.other_names: harbour of Barke before the refoundation; Tulmaytha (Arabic)
cities.site: Tolmeita, Marj District
cities.greek_from_text: small Greek harbour settlement from the late 7th or early 6th c. BC (archaeology), later the port of Barke ('the harbour of the Barkaians' in Pseudo-Scylax 108, 4th c. BC); refounded on the same site as the city of Ptolemais under the Ptolemies in the 3rd c. BC (Ptolemy III is usually named, though Ptolemy I has been proposed; its citizens are attested by c. 250 BC)
cities.until_text: Administration: capital of Libya Superior from c. 300; Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: occupation went on for centuries (glazed wares of the 10th-13th c.), but Greek after 643 is not attested. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
cities.fade_evidence: Synesius, bishop here c. 410-413, describes raids by the Ausurians (Austuriani) and the town under siege; the edict of Anastasius on the Libyan garrison (c. 501) was set up here; Justinian restored the aqueduct of a town half-deserted for lack of water (Procopius, Buildings 6.2.9-11); domestic occupation into the Islamic period (Ward-Perkins; Kennet 1991); no Greek text after 643.
cities.ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri). Earlier: the raids of the Ausurians (Austuriani) described by Synesius (405, 411-412) and the earthquake of 365 (natural). No named act ends Greek speech after 643.
cities.founder: Barke (as its harbour); refounded as Ptolemais by a Ptolemaic king (Ptolemy I, II or III; disputed)
cities.pre_greek_note: Before the refoundation the site was the Greek harbour of Barke; no pre-Greek settlement is known.
cities.status_evidence: Pentapolis city; Greek civic inscriptions (gymnasiarchs, ephebes); metropolis of Libya Superior; see (Secundus at Nicaea 325, Synesius c. 410-413, Evoptius 431, Georgius 553)
cities.note: The founder is disputed: a papyrus attesting citizens of Ptolemais by 252 BC rules out a foundation by Ptolemy III. Some accounts have the town destroyed and abandoned at the conquest; excavated pottery shows occupation into the Islamic period.
sources: Libyan Studies: 'Dating the Ptolemaic city-foundations in Cyrenaica'
cities.refoundations: Harbour of Barke -> Ptolemais (royal refoundation, mid-3rd c. BC; first papyrus naming its citizens 252 BC; same site)

cities.other_names: Arsinoe (Ἀρσινόη, Ptolemaic name after Arsinoe II); Teucheira (late-antique spelling); Tukra (Arabic)
cities.site: Tocra, Marj District
cities.greek_from_text: the earliest Greek pottery from the sanctuary deposit is of c. 620 BC (Boardman and Hayes); Herodotus (4.171) knows it as a city in the territory of Barke
cities.until_text: Administration: the Arab advance of 642/643 ended Roman rule; the date and manner of Teucheira's own surrender are not recorded. A modern reconstruction (Goodchild) makes Teucheira, which Justinian had strongly fortified, the last stronghold of the Roman forces, from which the garrison and the wealthier townspeople left by sea; the primary source for this evacuation is not securely identified and it should be treated as a hypothesis. Speech: the town lived on under Muslim rule to about the 10th c. (Arabic inscription in the bath), but there is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed: no Greek text of a resident is known from after 643, and al-Idrisi (12th c.) calls its people Berbers. The end date is that of the conquest, and the range allows for a remnant.
cities.fade_evidence: walls of the late 5th-6th c.; Procopius says Justinian strongly fortified Teucheira (Buildings 6.2.4); Greek inscriptions to the 6th c.; the evacuation of the garrison and the wealthy by sea after 642/643 is a modern reconstruction (Goodchild); Arabic inscription over the door of the bath (King 1989); al-Idrisi: Berber inhabitants.
cities.ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri). Goodchild put the town's fall in a later campaign, with the Roman forces and wealthy townspeople leaving by sea; the sources do not say how it fell. No named act ends Greek speech after 643.
cities.pre_greek_note: The name Taucheira is not Greek and may be Libyan, but it is known only from Greek and Latin sources.
cities.status_evidence: IACP 1029; Pentapolis city; see in late antiquity
cities.note: Recent work dates the walled compound once called the last monument of Roman rule to Anastasius rather than the 640s.
cities.refoundations: Renamed Arsinoe in the 3rd c. BC (same site), later Teucheira again

cities.site: near the mouth of Wadi Ka'am (Wadi Qaam, the ancient Cinyps river) between Al-Khums (Lepcis Magna) and Zliten, Murqub District; exact site unknown
cities.greek_from_text: colony founded on the Cinyps river by the Spartan prince Dorieus, son of King Anaxandridas, with Theraean guides (Hdt. 5.42); the date c. 515/514 BC is a modern reckoning from the accession of Cleomenes I; no archaeological trace of the settlement
cities.until_text: Speech and administration ended together: Herodotus says Dorieus settled 'the fairest spot in Libya, by the river', and was driven out in the third year; the colonists went back to the Peloponnese, and Dorieus later tried again in western Sicily (Herakleia near Eryx), where he was killed (Hdt. 5.42-46).
cities.fade_evidence: Hdt. 5.42 is the only evidence; rescue excavations in the Wadi Ka'am valley found a Punic and Roman cemetery (3rd c. BC - 1st c. AD) but nothing of the Spartan settlement.
cities.ended_by: Expelled in the third year by the Macae, other Libyans and the Carthaginians (Hdt. 5.42), c. 512 BC.
cities.founder: Dorieus of Sparta, son of Anaxandridas, with Theraean guides
cities.pre_greek_note: Cinyps (Κίνυψ) is the name of the river and of the Libyan district (Hdt. 4.175, 4.198); no non-Greek form is attested.
cities.status_evidence: Hdt. 5.42 (an organized colony under an oikist, sent out with Theraean guides); not an attested polis with known institutions
cities.note: A real but very short-lived colony (two to three years). Whether it ever functioned as a city with civic institutions is unknown, and it has not been located; it is kept as the only historical Greek foundation in Tripolitania.
sources: Pleiades 344413 (Kinyps, near the mouth of Wadi Caam)

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.other_names: Cirta Regia (royal seat of the Numidian kings); colonia Iulia Iuvenalis Honoris et Virtutis Cirta (Roman colony); Constantina (renamed by Constantine, 313); Qusantina (Arabic)
cities.site: Constantine (the Rhumel rock and the El Hofra sanctuary), Constantine Province
cities.greek_from_text: Greek settlers placed in the town by Micipsa, king of Numidia 148-118 BC (Strabo 17.3.13); Greek dedications at the El Hofra sanctuary of Baal Hammon, before the Roman conquest (2nd-1st c. BC)
cities.until_text: Administration: Numidian kings to 46 BC, then Rome. Speech: the Greek community is known only from Strabo's notice on Micipsa and the undated Greek stelae of El Hofra (the dated stelae run from 163/2 to c. 122/1 BC). In 112 BC Jugurtha took Cirta after a long siege and killed Adherbal, the adult Numidians and the foreign traders (Sall. Jug. 26.3); in 46 BC Caesar gave the town to P. Sittius and his men, and Roman Cirta, head of the four colonies, has a large and almost entirely Latin epigraphy. No Greek-speaking community is attested after the 2nd c. BC; the end date is an estimate.
cities.fade_evidence: Last datable El Hofra stelae c. 122/1 BC (Micipsa); Greek stelae individually undated; the Roman colony's inscriptions (CIL VIII, ILAlg II) are Latin.
cities.ended_by: No named act against the Greeks as such: Jugurtha took Cirta in 112 BC and massacred the adult Numidians and the negotiatores (Sall. Jug. 26.3), and Caesar handed the town to P. Sittius and his followers as a Roman colony in 46 BC (App. BC 4.54); whether the Greeks settled by Micipsa were among Jugurtha's victims is not recorded.
cities.founder: Micipsa, king of Numidia, settled Greeks in the existing royal town
cities.pre_greek_note: Cirta was the capital of Syphax and Masinissa before Micipsa (Livy 30.12); the name is native (Libyan or Punic) and is used in Greek and Latin without change; its Punic spelling is not given here.
cities.other_language: Punic (the written and court language of Numidian Cirta) and Libyan (Numidian)
cities.bilingual_evidence: FOR: Strabo 17.3.13 says King Micipsa 'settled a colony of Greeks in it' and made Cirta strong enough to send out 10,000 horse and twice as many foot; among the c. 700 stelae from the El Hofra sanctuary, 17 are inscribed in Greek beside c. 281 Punic and neo-Punic and 7 Latin, so Greek is the second language of the sanctuary (Greek and Latin stelae to Kronos and Tanit, before the Roman conquest: Le Glay 1966); modern accounts describe Micipsa's rebuilt Cirta as a mixed Libyan, Punic and Greek town, with Greek architects at court and refugees, including Greek mercenaries, after the fall of Carthage in 146 BC. AGAINST: no Greek civic institutions or coins; at least one Greek-script stele merely transliterates a Punic text, so some Greek writing comes from Punic speakers; the foreign traders who defended Cirta in 112 BC are called Italici (Sall. Jug. 21, 26).
cities.status_evidence: royal capital of the Numidian kings; Strabo 17.3.13 (Greek settlers); El Hofra Greek stelae (Berthier and Charlier 1955); later Roman colony and see
cities.note: Doubtful case. Strabo's notice is explicit and the El Hofra Greek share (c. 6% of the legible stelae) resembles Rome's, but it rests on one sanctuary and some Greek-script dedicants were Punic speakers; it is kept as the only North African town west of Cyrenaica with a recorded settlement of Greek residents.
sources: Berthier and Charlier, Le sanctuaire punique d'El-Hofra a Constantine (1955)
Le Glay, Saturne africain. Monuments II (1966)
cities.refoundations: Roman colony of P. Sittius, 46 BC; renamed Constantina by Constantine, 313 (same site)

cities.period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
cities.other_names: Ptolemais of the Hunts; Ptolemais Epitheras (Pliny 6.171); Ptolemais in Troglodytis (Pliny 2.183)
cities.site: unlocated; most likely at Aqiq (Khor Aqiq), Red Sea State, Sudan; Trinkitat, Suakin (Sudan) and Arqiqo (Eritrea) have also been proposed
cities.greek_from_text: founded for Ptolemy II by Eumedes, whom the king sent to the elephant-hunting grounds: he enclosed a peninsula with a ditch and a wall and won over the natives who tried to stop him (Strabo 16.4.7); the Pithom stele (l. 22-24), under year 16 (270/269 BC), records 'a great city' with the king's name built by the general who caught elephants for him, usually taken as this foundation
cities.until_text: Founded as the base of the royal elephant hunt. Administration: the hunts were run by royal commanders and soldiers under Ptolemy II-IV; they were cut off by the Great Revolt of the Thebaid (205-186 BC), which closed the Koptos-Berenike route, and ended in the 2nd c. BC, at the latest when Ptolemy VI's revived programme stopped at his death in 145 (Burstein). Speech: no Greek residents are attested after the hunting period. By c. AD 40-70 the Periplus (ch. 3) knows it only as a small trading place without a harbour, reached by small boats, selling tortoiseshell and a little ivory, on a coast under Zoskales, king of the Aksumites (ch. 5); Greek traders who came by sea from Egypt were visitors, not residents. The end date is an estimate.
cities.fade_evidence: Pithom stele, year 16 (270/269 BC); dedications by the commanders of Ptolemy IV's elephant hunts found in Egypt (OGIS 82-86); noon-shadow observations at Ptolemais reported by Eratosthenes and Pliny (NH 2.183); Agatharchides (c. 145-132 BC) on the hunting coast; Periplus 3 (c. AD 40-70): a small trading place; Ptolemy, Geography 4.7.7 (c. AD 150) still lists it.
cities.ended_by: No named act: the elephant hunts for which the town was founded were cut off by the Great Revolt of the Thebaid under the native pharaohs Haronnophris and Chaonnophris (205-186 BC) and given up by the Ptolemies in the 2nd c. BC, at the latest after the death of Ptolemy VI (145 BC); by the 1st c. AD the coast lay under Zoskales, king of the Aksumites (Periplus 5).
cities.pre_greek_note: Strabo says Eumedes built on a peninsula and won over local people who resisted; no earlier settlement or native name is attested.
cities.status_evidence: royal foundation: 'a city founded by Eumedes' (Strabo 16.4.7); Pithom stele l. 23, 'a great city with the name of the king'; 'oppidum' in Pliny, NH 6.171; listed by Ptolemy, Geography 4.7.7; Cohen 2006
cities.note: The site is not securely located: Aqiq is favoured by Burstein and a Russian-Sudanese survey of 2025 found 3rd-c. BC pottery there, but the identification is unproven. The foundation is well attested, but whether a Greek civic community lived there beyond the king's hunters and soldiers is not documented.
sources: Pithom stele, l. 22-24 (year 16 of Ptolemy II)

left_out.name: Thonis-Herakleion (Θῶνις / Ἡράκλειον)
left_out.reason: Emporion and customs post at the Canopic mouth with a temple of Amun-Gereb/Herakles (Hdt. 2.113; Naukratis stela of 380 BC); no civic status; declined from the 2nd c. BC and later submerged. Greek traders lived there, but it was never a city.

left_out.name: Plinthine (Kom el-Nugus)
left_out.reason: Egyptian town on the Mareotic ridge (Hellanicus; Hdt. 2.6 'Plinthinetic gulf') with Greek imports from the 7th c. BC; no evidence of civic status or of a Greek-speaking civic community.

left_out.name: Marea / Mareia (Μάρεια)
left_out.reason: Egyptian border fortress and town (Hdt. 2.18, 2.30; Thuc. 1.104); in the Roman period part of Alexandria's territory (the Mareotes): Athanasius says the Mareotis never had a bishop or city (Apol. c. Ar. 85); the Arian bishops Ischyras (c. 338) and Pistos were not a regular see. Its large late antique harbour town at Hawwariya (often identified with Philoxenite, the pilgrim station for Abu Mina) had no civic status.

left_out.name: Philoxenite (Hawwariya)
left_out.reason: Late 5th-6th c. pilgrim town and harbour on Lake Mareotis serving Abu Mina; no civic status.

left_out.name: Abu Mina (shrine of St Menas)
left_out.reason: Pilgrimage sanctuary with a 6th-c. town; no bishop or civic status attested.

left_out.name: Menouthis
left_out.reason: Village near Kanopos with the shrine of Isis and later of Cyrus and John; a village, not a city (treated under Kanopos).

left_out.name: Menelaos (city of Menelaus near Kanopos)
left_out.reason: Named by Strabo 17.1.18 as eponym of the Menelaite nome, but unlocated; the late Roman see of the Menelaites is treated under Schedia and the district under Kanopos.

left_out.name: Rhakotis
left_out.reason: Not a separate city: the Egyptian name (Ra-Kedet) of the site or quarter of Alexandria; treated under Alexandria.

left_out.name: Eleusis (near Alexandria)
left_out.reason: Suburb of Alexandria (Polybius, Livy, Strabo); no civic status.

left_out.name: Bolbitine (Rosetta area)
left_out.reason: Town at the Bolbitine mouth named by Herodotus and Strabo; no civic status or bishop attested before the Arab conquest (the see of Rashid is medieval).

left_out.name: Kom el-Hisn (Imau)
left_out.reason: Egyptian town; may be the site of Gynaikopolis or Momemphis, which are entered under their Greek names.

left_out.name: Kom Firin
left_out.reason: Egyptian fortress and temple town of the western Delta with Roman occupation; no civic status attested under any Greek name (an identification with Phragonis is unproven).

left_out.name: Behbeit el-Hagar (Iseion, Isidis oppidum)
left_out.reason: Temple of Isis near Samannud; a sanctuary and village, not a city.

left_out.name: Nitriote nome (Wadi el-Natrun)
left_out.reason: The Nitriote district (Strabo 17.1.23) had no known metropolis; its monastic settlements (Nitria, Kellia, Scetis) belonged to the see of Hermopolis Parva and were not cities.

left_out.name: Boukolia
left_out.reason: District see of the northern Delta marshes named in episcopal lists, without a known town; the possibly related see of Elearchia is entered separately.

left_out.name: Prosopis
left_out.reason: A city of this name is attested only in late sources and may never have existed; the Prosopite metropolis was Nikiou (entered).

left_out.name: Stratopeda (camps of the Ionians and Carians)
left_out.reason: Military camps of Psamtik I's Greek and Carian mercenaries on the Pelusiac branch (Hdt. 2.154), in the eastern Delta, outside this region; camps, not cities.

left_out.name: Pharos
left_out.reason: Island and lighthouse of Alexandria, joined to the city by the Heptastadion; part of Alexandria, not a separate city.

left_out.name: Daphnai (Tell Defenna)
left_out.reason: Saite frontier fortress 'Daphnai of Pelusium' with Greek (and Carian) mercenaries and much Greek pottery (Hdt. 2.30, 2.107; Petrie 1886), 7th-6th c. BC; a garrison, not a city. Tahpanhes of Jeremiah. Its identification with the late antique Aphnaion is not secure.

left_out.name: Aphnaion (Aphnaeum)
left_out.reason: Listed among the cities of Augustamnica I by Hierocles and later a titular see, but no bishop, inscription or resident is attested for it, so there is no positive evidence of a Greek-speaking community; site unknown (perhaps Tell Defenna).

left_out.name: Pentaschoinon
left_out.reason: Road station on the coast road east of Pelusium, listed by Hierocles but with no bishop, inscription or resident attested; no positive evidence of a Greek-speaking civic community.

left_out.name: Skenai within and outside Gerrha
left_out.reason: Listed by Hierocles as two places beside Gerrha; road settlements of Gerrha without separate evidence; folded into Gerrha.

left_out.name: Magdolos (Migdol; Tell el-Herr)
left_out.reason: Frontier fortress (Hdt. 2.159; Tell el-Herr, a Persian, Ptolemaic and Roman fort) and later the station Magdolum; a fort, not a city.

left_out.name: Thou
left_out.reason: Roman road station and fort in the eastern Delta (Itinerarium Antonini; Notitia Dignitatum, 'Thohu'); no civic status or Greek community attested.

left_out.name: Skenai Mandrai (Scenae Mandrae)
left_out.reason: Roman military post (Notitia Dignitatum) near the head of the Delta; no civic status attested.

left_out.name: Scenae Veteranorum
left_out.reason: Roman road station and veterans' post in the Heliopolite area (Itinerarium Antonini; Notitia Dignitatum); no civic status.

left_out.name: Leontopolis of Onias (Oniou; Tell el-Yahudiya)
left_out.reason: Jewish military settlement and temple founded by the priest Onias IV, c. 160 BC, in the Heliopolite nome ('the land of Onias'); its residents spoke Greek (Greek epitaphs, JIGRE 29-105), but it was a military colony and temple settlement that Josephus calls a small town (polichne), without civic status; the temple was closed by Lupus and Paulinus on Vespasian's order, AD 73/74 (Jos. BJ 7.420-436).

left_out.name: Aphroditopolis (Delta)
left_out.reason: The Delta Aphroditopolis (Atarbechis, Hdt. 2.41) lay on the Prosopite island in the central-western Delta, outside this area; known only as a cult town, with no civic status or Greek community attested.

left_out.name: Phelbes (Bilbeis)
left_out.reason: Later a titular see of Augustamnica II, and a fortified town taken by 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640 after a siege, but no ancient bishop, inscription or resident Greek-speaking community is attested in the sources consulted.

left_out.name: Shata
left_out.reason: Town near Damietta known as a see only from the Arab period (Coptic sources); no Greek-period civic evidence.

left_out.name: Hermopolis of the 15th Lower Egyptian nome (Baqliya)
left_out.reason: Old Egyptian nome capital (Ba'h, Tell el-Naqus) with no attested Greek-period metropolis, see or Greek community; not to be confused with Hermopolis Parva (Damanhur) in the western Delta.

left_out.name: Raphia (Rafah)
left_out.reason: Out of area: the ancient city lies under Rafah in the Gaza Strip (Palaestina Prima); the modern border divides only the later town.

left_out.name: Monastery of Sinai (St Catherine)
left_out.reason: Fortified monastery built under Justinian (c. 548-565) with Greek-speaking monks to this day; a monastery, not a city.

left_out.name: Raithou (El-Tor)
left_out.reason: Monastic settlement and small port with a fort in South Sinai; no civic status or see.

left_out.name: Avaris / Pi-Ramesse (Tell el-Dab'a, Qantir)
left_out.reason: Bronze Age capitals abandoned long before the Greek period.

left_out.name: Ptolemais Hormou (El-Lahun, Fayum)
left_out.reason: Ptolemaic harbour of the Fayum at the entrance of the Bahr Yusuf; despite the name it was a village (kome) of the Arsinoite in the papyri, with no gymnasium, boule or see; Greek-speaking residents but no civic status.

left_out.name: Philadelpheia (Kom el-Kharaba el-Kebir, Fayum)
left_out.reason: Greek-speaking village founded under Ptolemy II (Zenon archive); a kome of the Arsinoite, never a city.

left_out.name: Karanis (Kom Aushim, Fayum)
left_out.reason: Large Greek-speaking village of the Arsinoite; no civic status.

left_out.name: Tebtunis (Umm el-Breigat, Fayum)
left_out.reason: Village of the Arsinoite (temple of Soknebtunis, Greek and Demotic papyri); sometimes proposed as the site of Theodosiopolis, which is doubted; listed under Theodosiopolis (Arcadia) only as a candidate site.

left_out.name: Soknopaiou Nesos (Dime, Fayum)
left_out.reason: Temple village of the Arsinoite with mostly Demotic and Greek temple documents; no civic status.

left_out.name: Bakchias (Kom Umm el-Atl, Fayum)
left_out.reason: Village of the Arsinoite; no civic status.

left_out.name: Dionysias (Qasr Qarun, Fayum)
left_out.reason: Village of the Arsinoite with a late Roman fort; no civic status.

left_out.name: Other Fayum villages (Narmouthis, Theadelpheia, Euhemeria, Philoteris, Kerkeosiris, Magdola)
left_out.reason: Greek-speaking villages of the Arsinoite founded or settled under the Ptolemies; none had civic status.

left_out.name: Ankyronon polis (el-Hiba)
left_out.reason: Fortified village of the Herakleopolite (source of the Hibeh papyri); no civic status or see.

left_out.name: Hipponon
left_out.reason: Village and late Roman fort station (Notitia Dignitatum) in Middle Egypt; no civic status; exact site disputed.

left_out.name: Akoris (Tehna el-Gebel)
left_out.reason: Important Ptolemaic and Roman town with Greek dedications, but a village (kome) in the papyri; no boule, see or entry in Hierocles.

left_out.name: Alabastrine / Alabastron polis
left_out.reason: Village by the alabaster quarries in the Hermopolite-Antinoite area; 'polis' only in its name; no civic status.

left_out.name: Tilothis
left_out.reason: Same place as Nilopolis (Coptic Tiloj, modern Dalas); entered under Nilopolis.

left_out.name: Ibion
left_out.reason: Name of several villages of the Arsinoite and Hermopolite (Ibion Eikosipentarouron and others); no civic status.

left_out.name: Pempte
left_out.reason: Village known from papyri; no civic status, see or Greek civic institutions.

left_out.name: Saqqara (Serapeum of Memphis)
left_out.reason: Sanctuary and necropolis of Memphis; included under Memphis, not a city.

left_out.name: Akanthos (Dahshur)
left_out.reason: Village and sanctuary of the Memphite nome; no civic status.

left_out.name: Alphocranon (placed at Helwan by the modern list of titular sees)
left_out.reason: The name is a corruption of Phragonis, a see with bishops 325-458 that the checklists place at al-Farragin, outside this area; no ancient city at Helwan is attested.

left_out.name: Oasis Parva (Bahariya, Giza Governorate)
left_out.reason: District of the Small Oasis linked to the Oxyrhynchite; Greek officials and soldiers, but no city with civic status or Greek-speaking civic community is attested; left to any Western Desert listing.

left_out.name: Thinis (This), near Girga (El-Birba?), Sohag Governorate
left_out.reason: Old capital of the Thinite nome, site not securely located; from the Ptolemaic period the centre of the nome was the Greek city Ptolemais Hermiou. No Greek civic institutions or Greek-speaking civic community attested at Thinis itself; its modern listing as a titular see does not establish one.

left_out.name: Abydos (Ἄβυδος), Sohag Governorate
left_out.reason: Temple and pilgrimage centre (the Memnonion, oracle of Bes) in the territory of Ptolemais; the many Greek graffiti are by visitors. Never a nome metropolis or see with civic institutions in the Greek period.

left_out.name: Athribis / Triphieion (Wannina), Sohag Governorate
left_out.reason: Temple town of the Panopolite nome; village without civic status.

left_out.name: Lepidotonpolis (Nag el-Mashayikh), Sohag Governorate
left_out.reason: Small temple town/village of the Thinite district; no civic status.

left_out.name: Chenoboskion (Sheneset, Qasr es-Sayed), Qena Governorate
left_out.reason: Village; known for Pachomius' early monastery and the Nag Hammadi codices found nearby; no civic status.

left_out.name: Tabennese and Pbow (Faw Qibli), Qena Governorate
left_out.reason: Villages and Pachomian monasteries (Coptic-speaking communities); no civic status.

left_out.name: Krokodilopolis (Gebelein), Luxor Governorate
left_out.reason: Garrison settlement on the second hill of Gebelein, twin of Pathyris; a village, not a nome metropolis. Its Greek soldiers are covered under Pathyris.

left_out.name: Memnonia / Djeme (Medinet Habu, Theban west bank), Luxor Governorate
left_out.reason: District and village (kastron Memnonion; Coptic town of Djeme, 6th-8th c.) within the territory of Thebes; not a city in its own right. Its documents are used under Thebes.

left_out.name: Medamud (Madu), Luxor Governorate
left_out.reason: Temple village of the Theban nome; no civic status.

left_out.name: Tuphium (Tod), Luxor Governorate
left_out.reason: Village of the Hermonthite nome; no civic status.

left_out.name: Asphynis (Asfun el-Mata'na), Luxor Governorate
left_out.reason: Village; no civic status.

left_out.name: Eileithyiaspolis (Elkab), Aswan Governorate
left_out.reason: Pharaonic nome capital (Nekheb), in the Greek period a temple town between Latopolis and Apollonopolis Magna; Greek texts there are mainly visitors' graffiti. No metropolis status, see or Greek civic institutions attested.

left_out.name: Hierakonpolis (Nekhen, Kom el-Ahmar), Aswan Governorate
left_out.reason: Pharaonic town, small and of no civic status in the Greek and Roman periods.

left_out.name: Silsilis (Gebel el-Silsila), Aswan Governorate
left_out.reason: Sandstone quarries with a garrison post and shrines; not a city.

left_out.name: Contra Syene, Contrapollonopolis, Contra Latopolis
left_out.reason: Garrison posts on the bank opposite the cities (Notitia dignitatum); not cities.

left_out.name: Elephantine (Yebu), Aswan Governorate
left_out.reason: Fortress island (phrourion) opposite Syene; its Greek settlers (P.Eleph. 1, 311 BC) and the late Roman soldier families of the Patermouthis archive are counted under Syene, which was the civic centre and see.

left_out.name: Philae (Φίλαι), Aswan Governorate
left_out.reason: Temple island with a late Roman garrison; bishops of Philae are attested from the 4th c. (Macedonius) but there were no civic institutions, and the Greek texts are by officials, soldiers, pilgrims and the bishop rather than a resident Greek-speaking community. The temple of Isis was closed by Narses under Justinian (c. 537; Procopius, Wars 1.19).

left_out.name: Leukos Limen (Quseir?)
left_out.reason: Harbour listed by Ptolemy (Geog. 4.5); no town with civic status or Greek residents attested, and the identification with El-Quseir or with Quseir al-Qadim is disputed (Quseir al-Qadim is now Myos Hormos).

left_out.name: Nechesia (Marsa Nakari?)
left_out.reason: Harbour in Ptolemy's list; the Ptolemaic-Roman settlement at Marsa Nakari is a small harbour station, not a city.

left_out.name: Abu Sha'ar
left_out.reason: Late Roman fort (building inscription of 309/311), later a Christian pilgrimage place; a fort, not a city.

left_out.name: Mons Porphyrites (Gebel Abu Dukhan)
left_out.reason: Imperial porphyry quarry with workers' settlement and forts; quarry, not a city.

left_out.name: Mons Claudianus
left_out.reason: Imperial granite quarry with fortified workers' camp; quarry, not a city.

left_out.name: Mons Smaragdus (Sikait, Senskis and the emerald mines)
left_out.reason: Mining settlements; no civic status.

left_out.name: Bir Umm Fawakhir
left_out.reason: Late Roman gold-mining settlement (5th-6th c.) on the Koptos-Quseir road; mining town, not a city.

left_out.name: Praesidia and hydreumata of the Eastern Desert roads (Didymoi, Maximianon, Krokodilo, Persou, Phoinikon, Aphrodites Oros, Dios, Xeron Pelagos, Kompasi, Apollonos Hydreuma, Kainon Hydreuma, Vetus Hydreuma and others)
left_out.reason: Ptolemaic and Roman forts and watering stations; Greek ostraca were written by soldiers and travellers, not by a civic community.

left_out.name: Shenshef and Hitan Rayan
left_out.reason: Late Roman desert settlements near Berenike, probably linked to Blemmyan groups; villages, not cities.

left_out.name: Mersa Gawasis (Saww)
left_out.reason: Pharaonic Red Sea harbour; no Greek city (sometimes proposed for Philotera, see that entry).

left_out.name: Berenike Panchrysos
left_out.reason: Ptolemaic gold-mining settlement, probably Deraheib in the Wadi Allaqi near the Sudan border; mining town, not a city.

left_out.name: Arsinoe Trogodytike and other Ptolemaic harbours south of Berenike
left_out.reason: Unlocated or on the Sudanese and Eritrean coast (other regions); no evidence of towns with Greek residents on the Egyptian coast.

left_out.name: Monasteries of St Antony and St Paul
left_out.reason: Monasteries, not cities.

left_out.name: Kysis (Dush)
left_out.reason: Village with a fort and temple in the Kharga Oasis; Greek ostraca (O. Douch) of villagers and soldiers, but no civic status.

left_out.name: Other Kharga sites (Qasr el-Ghueita, Qasr Zayyan/Tchonemyris, Mounesis/Shams el-Din, Ain el-Labakha, Umm el-Dabadib, El-Deir, Ain Manawir)
left_out.reason: Villages, temples and forts, not cities.

left_out.name: Bagawat
left_out.reason: Christian necropolis of Hibis; part of the Hibis entry.

left_out.name: Ibis
left_out.reason: Variant spelling of Hibis; merged into that entry.

left_out.name: Kellis (Ismant el-Kharab)
left_out.reason: Village of the Mothite nome, abandoned c. 400; famous Greek and Coptic papyri but never a city.

left_out.name: Other Dakhla sites (Ain el-Gedida, Deir el-Hagar, Ain Birbiya, Mesobe)
left_out.reason: Villages and temples, not cities.

left_out.name: Farafra
left_out.reason: Small oasis with Roman-period villages (Ain Besay, Qasr Farafra); no town with civic status or Greek community.

left_out.name: Bahariya forts and villages (El-Bawiti necropolis, Qaret el-Toub, El-Haiz, Bir Shawish)
left_out.reason: Necropolis, Roman fort and villages; the chief place is treated under Psobthis.

left_out.name: Ammonion (Siwa Oasis: Aghurmi, Umm Ubayda, Gebel el-Mawta)
left_out.reason: Oracle sanctuary of Ammon in a Libyan-speaking oasis; Greek visitors and dedications and a Greek-style tomb (Si-Amun) but no Greek-speaking civic community; a see 'Ammoniace' appears only in modern titular lists; Siwi (Berber) is spoken there today.

left_out.name: Qara and other small oases of the Matrouh interior
left_out.reason: No ancient city attested.

left_out.name: Balagrai (Balagrae, Al Bayda)
left_out.reason: Sanctuary of Asclepius and village in the territory of Cyrene; no civic institutions, coinage or see attested.

left_out.name: Hydrax
left_out.reason: Village; Synesius (Ep. 67) calls Hydrax and Palaebisca two villages of the Pentapolis on the frontier of arid Libya, briefly given their own bishop (Siderius) and then returned to the see of Erythron.

left_out.name: Palaebisca
left_out.reason: Village (Synesius, Ep. 67); a short-lived bishopric with Hydrax, not a city.

left_out.name: Phykous (Ras al-Hilal area, Zawiet el-Hamama)
left_out.reason: Cape and anchorage of Cyrene (Strabo 17.3.20); no civic status.

left_out.name: Naustathmos (El Hania)
left_out.reason: Anchorage and road station east of Apollonia; no civic status.

left_out.name: Kainopolis (Cenopolis)
left_out.reason: Known only as a name in Ptolemy and on the Peutinger Table; site and status unknown, no evidence of a civic community.

left_out.name: Boreion (Boreum)
left_out.reason: Procopius (Buildings 6.2.12-23) calls it the westernmost city of the Pentapolis, unwalled and untaxed, with an old Jewish community whose temple Justinian made a church; later a see; no positive evidence of a Greek-speaking civic community (no Greek inscriptions, coins or bishops of the town).

left_out.name: Lasamikes
left_out.reason: Village or station in Ptolemy; no civic status.

left_out.name: Zygris (Zawiyet el-Hamam?)
left_out.reason: A see of Libya Inferior (bishops Marcus 362, Lucius 449), but Ptolemy calls it a village and there is no positive evidence of a resident Greek-speaking civic community; location uncertain.

left_out.name: Zagylis
left_out.reason: A see of Libya Inferior (bishops 449, 457, c. 480) whose site is unknown; no positive evidence of a Greek-speaking civic community.

left_out.name: Dysthis (Dystis)
left_out.reason: A see of Libya Superior (bishops Samuel 431, Petrus 458) whose site is unknown; it cannot be placed on a map and no evidence of the town itself survives.

left_out.name: Paliouros (Paliurus, Timimi)
left_out.reason: Village or station in Ptolemy and the itineraries; no civic status.

left_out.name: Apis (west of Marsa Matruh)
left_out.reason: Border town of Libyans and Egyptians (Hdt. 2.18); no positive evidence of a Greek-speaking civic community.

left_out.name: Augila (Awjila)
left_out.reason: Libyan oasis (Hdt. 4.172); Procopius (Buildings 6.2.14-20) has its people worship Ammon until Justinian converted them and built a church of the Mother of God; no Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Jalu oasis
left_out.reason: No ancient city attested; Libyan oasis.

left_out.name: Arae Philaenorum
left_out.reason: Boundary monument and road station on the Gulf of Sirte between Carthaginian and Cyrenaean territory; no civic status.

left_out.name: Automala
left_out.reason: Fort and station on the Gulf of Sirte; no civic status.

left_out.name: Corniclanum / Ajdabiya
left_out.reason: Roman road station; the town of Ajdabiya is an Arab-period foundation (al-Ya'qubi, al-Bakri).

left_out.name: Katabathmos Megas (Sollum)
left_out.reason: Pass and boundary station between Egypt and Libya; no civic status.

left_out.name: Menelaos harbour (Menelai Portus)
left_out.reason: Harbour of Marmarica (where Agesilaos II died, 360/359 BC); no civic status.

left_out.name: Leuke Akte
left_out.reason: Cape and harbour on the Marmarican coast; no civic status.

left_out.name: Bates's Island (Marsa Matruh)
left_out.reason: Late Bronze Age trading camp with Cypriot and Aegean pottery; not a Greek settlement or city (noted under Paraitonion).

left_out.name: Leukaspis
left_out.reason: Harbour named by Strabo and Ptolemy; possibly the same excavated town as Antiphrai at Marina el-Alamein, entered there.

left_out.name: Marmarica (see of Theonas, 325)
left_out.reason: A see named after the region, held by Theonas at Nicaea; its town is not identified.

left_out.name: Slonta
left_out.reason: Libyan rock sanctuary in the Jabal al Akhdar; not a city.

left_out.name: Agriolode and Dinarthisum
left_out.reason: Monasteries fortified by Justinian on the southern edge of the Pentapolis (Procopius, Buildings 6.2.7-8); not cities.

left_out.name: Carthage (Qart-hadasht; Karchedon; Carthago), Tunis, Tunisia
left_out.reason: Punic, then Latin city (renamed Iustiniane under Justinian, Procopius, Aed. 6.5.8); Greek is not shown to have been one of its two main languages in any period. Punic period: a Greek resident community existed (in 396 BC, after the plague at Syracuse, the Carthaginians adopted the cult of Demeter and Kore and 'chose out the most prominent Greeks who lived among them' for the service of the goddesses, Diod. 14.77.5; Greek mercenaries, wives and tutors of the elite), but Justin 20.5.12-13 records a decree that no Carthaginian should study Greek letters or speech after a traitor wrote to Dionysius I in Greek, which shows Greek was a learned language, not a common one; Punic was the city's language until its destruction by Scipio Aemilianus in 146 BC. Roman colony (44 BC, settled under Augustus): Latin and Punic; Greek appears as an educated or immigrant language (Apuleius' Greek and Latin hymn, Florida 18; Tertullian's lost Greek works; Perpetua speaks Greek with the bishop Optatus and the priest Aspasius in her vision, Passio 13), and Greek epitaphs are a small minority of the city's funerary inscriptions. Under Constantinople (533-698): the Greek of exarchs, officials and garrison does not count; Greek-speaking civilians are attested (Eastern monks such as Maximus the Confessor, near Carthage from c. 630, who disputed in Greek with the ex-patriarch Pyrrhus at Carthage in 645 before the exarch Gregory and African bishops; refugees from Syria, Palestine and Egypt, including anti-Chalcedonian nuns from Alexandria, Maximus Ep. 12; the Greek-speaking Eastern Jews forcibly baptized in Carthage in the Greek Doctrina Jacobi, set in 634), but the African church wrote Latin (the councils and letters of 646), the townspeople spoke Latin, and the Greek-speaking administrators were a 'minute fraction' of the population (Conant, Staying Roman, 2012). A Greek-speaking immigrant minority, not a bilingual city (doubtful call for the 7th c.). Hassan ibn al-Nu'man took Carthage in 695, the patrician John retook it by sea in 697, and Hassan took and destroyed it in 698. Ancient DNA, which is evidence of ancestry and not of language: the genomes of 17 people from Carthage and 27 from nearby Kerkouane, of the Punic period, show mostly a Sicilian-Aegean-like ancestry, a minority of North African ancestry and almost no ancestry from the Levant (Ringbauer et al., Nature 643, 2025; for Kerkouane also Moots et al., Nature Ecology and Evolution 2023). The data cannot tell Sicily and the Aegean apart, and the authors name contact with the Greek colonies of the central Mediterranean and Cyrenaica as one possible source. It does not show what language these people spoke, so it does not change the decision; it does raise the possibility that Greeks were among the city's inhabitants, perhaps adopting its language and culture, an episode of linguistic conversion either in Africa or in the source of these genetically Aegean-Sicilian people.

left_out.name: Hadrumetum / Iustiniane (Sousse, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Phoenician-Punic town, then Roman colony and capital of Byzacena, renamed Iustiniane under Justinian (Procopius, Aed. 6.6.1-7); Latin and Punic. Greek appears only in magic (Greek curse tablets and the Greek love charm of the 3rd c. AD, Audollent DT 271) and in imperial administration; besieged by Agathocles c. 310 BC (Diod. 20) only as a military episode. No resident Greek-speaking community attested.

left_out.name: Utica (Henchir Bou Chateur, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Phoenician colony, then Punic town and capital of Roman Africa before Carthage; Latin and Punic. Stormed by Agathocles in 307 BC (Diod. 20.54-55), a military act only; no Greek settlers or Greek civic evidence.

left_out.name: Lepcis Magna (Lpqy; 'Neapolis' in Strabo 17.3.18; Al-Khums, Libya)
left_out.reason: Punic town, then Roman municipium and colony; its bilingual inscriptions are Punic-Latin (Annobal Tapapius Rufus, 8 BC and AD 1/2); the Greek name Neapolis is a geographers' name. A few Greek dedications are by visitors or for the Severan court; no resident Greek-speaking community attested. Raided by the Austuriani in 363-365 (Amm. 28.6); under Constantinople from 533; reached by the Arab campaign of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 642/643.

left_out.name: Oea (Wy't; Tripoli, Libya)
left_out.reason: Punic-Latin town. Apuleius (Apology 82-87, 98) shows a rich local family using Greek in letters (Pudentilla) and a son, Pudens, who spoke only Punic and a little Greek and no Latin: elite learned Greek, not a Greek-speaking community. Taken by 'Amr ibn al-'As after a siege of about a month in 643 (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam).

left_out.name: Sabratha (Sbrtn; 'Abrotonon' in Greek geographers; Sabratha, Libya)
left_out.reason: Punic town, then Roman municipium and colony; Punic and Latin. The Greek name Abrotonon (Strabo 17.3.18; Pliny 5.25) and the Hellenistic style of Mausoleum B do not show Greek speakers; Apuleius was tried here (c. 158/9). No Greek civic evidence. Taken by 'Amr ibn al-'As's troops after Oea, 643.

left_out.name: Gigthis (Bou Ghara, Medenine, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Punic emporion, then Roman municipium; Latin inscriptions; no Greek evidence.

left_out.name: Tacapae (Gabes, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Punic-Roman port town and later see; Latin and Punic; no Greek-speaking community attested.

left_out.name: Thapsus (Ras Dimass, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Punic-Roman town (battle of Thapsus, 46 BC); taken by Agathocles c. 310 BC (Diod. 20) as a military act only; no Greek civic evidence.

left_out.name: Leptis Minor (Lamta, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Punic-Roman town; Latin and Punic; no Greek evidence.

left_out.name: Neapolis (Nabeul, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Carthaginian emporion with a Greek name, used by Greek sailors as the nearest African port to Sicily (Thuc. 7.50.2, 413 BC); Punic, then Roman colony; no Greek residents attested.

left_out.name: Kerkouane (Cap Bon, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Punic town with Greek architectural and ceramic influence; abandoned in the mid-3rd c. BC (probably during the Roman invasion of 256-255 BC); no Greek inscriptions or Greek residents attested.

left_out.name: Meninx / Girba (island of Djerba, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Punic-Roman town and see on the island the Greek geographers identified with Homer's land of the Lotus-eaters (Strabo 17.3.17); a literary identification only, not a Greek settlement; Latin and Punic.

left_out.name: Cercina (Kerkennah islands, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Punic-Roman island town and see; no Greek evidence.

left_out.name: Hippo Regius (Annaba, Algeria)
left_out.reason: Punic-Numidian royal town, then Roman municipium and see of Augustine; Latin and Punic (Augustine on Punic speakers in his diocese, Ep. 108, 209); Augustine himself learned Greek only poorly (Conf. 1.13-14). No Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Caesarea / Iol (Cherchell, Algeria)
left_out.reason: Punic Iol refounded as Caesarea by Juba II (25 BC - AD 23) and Cleopatra Selene, whose court was Greek in culture (Greek legends on the queen's coins, Greek scholars and artists, Juba's Greek books); but a court is not enough. The town's large epigraphy is overwhelmingly Latin and Greek inscriptions are few; no Greek civic institutions or resident Greek-speaking community attested. Roman colony under Claudius (c. 40/42). Doubtful only in that the royal household included Greek-speaking freedmen.

left_out.name: Tipasa (Algeria)
left_out.reason: Punic trading town, then Latin municipium and colony; Latin epigraphy; no Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Volubilis (near Moulay Idriss, Morocco)
left_out.reason: Mauretanian (Libyan-Punic) town, then Roman municipium; Punic, Libyan and Latin inscriptions; its Hellenistic bronzes are imported art, not evidence of Greek speakers. No Greek community attested.

left_out.name: Lixus (Larache, Morocco)
left_out.reason: Phoenician-Punic town, then Roman colony; the Greek myths placed here (Antaeus, the Garden of the Hesperides, Pliny 5.3) are legends; no Greek settlement.

left_out.name: Tingi (Tangier, Morocco)
left_out.reason: Mauretanian-Punic town, then Roman colony; the Antaeus and Sophax foundation story (Plut. Sert. 9) is legend; Latin. No Greek community.

left_out.name: Septem / Septem Fratres (Ceuta)
left_out.reason: Out of area: Ceuta belongs to Spain. In any case a fort of the emperors in Constantinople with a garrison only (Procopius, Aed. 6.7.14-15).

left_out.name: Rusaddir (Melilla)
left_out.reason: Out of area: Melilla belongs to Spain; a Punic-Roman town in any case.

left_out.name: Aspis / Clupea (Kelibia, Nabeul, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Strabo 17.3.16 says Agathocles 'colonised' (synoikise) the hill of Aspis when he invaded Africa (310-307 BC), and Solinus 27.8 ascribes it to Sicilians; but there was a Punic town there, Agathocles' occupation was a military base held for at most three years, and when he left in 307 BC his army in Africa gave back the towns it held, was enrolled by Carthage or shipped to Solous in Sicily, and those who resisted were stormed (Diod. 20.69). Punic again (taken by Regulus in 256 BC, Polyb. 1.29), then a Roman colony. No resident Greek community. Doubtful call.

left_out.name: Hippou Akra / Hippo Diarrhytus (Bizerte, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Phoenician-Punic town stormed by Agathocles in 307 BC (Diod. 20.55.3), a military act only; then Roman colony and Latin see. No Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Kybos (Κύβος), 'a city of the Ionians in Phoenician Libya' (Hecataeus in Stephanus of Byzantium)
left_out.reason: Known only from one lexicon entry quoting Hecataeus; unlocated; no other text, coin or archaeology. Unsupported claim.

left_out.name: Karikon Teichos ('Carian Wall') and the other towns of Hanno's Periplus (Thymiaterion, Gytte, Akra, Melitta, Arambys), Atlantic Morocco
left_out.reason: Carthaginian foundations; the Greek names are the Greek translation of a Punic report. Not Greek settlements.

left_out.name: Kerne and Mogador (Essaouira, Morocco)
left_out.reason: Phoenician-Punic trading post (Ps.-Scylax 112 describes Phoenician traders at Kerne); a few Greek pots among the Phoenician finds at Mogador show trade, not Greek residents.

left_out.name: Charax and the Tower of Euphrantas (Gulf of Sirte, Libya)
left_out.reason: Charax was a Carthaginian emporion for smuggled Cyrenaic silphium, and Euphrantas' tower a frontier landmark (Strabo 17.3.20). Greek names, no Greek settlement or civic status.

left_out.name: Pithekoussai of Numidia (Diod. 20.58)
left_out.reason: Three native towns named by the Greeks after their monkeys; Agathocles' general Eumachus destroyed one and won over the other two (Diod. 20.58); Greek name only, no Greek settlement.

left_out.name: Lake Tritonis and the 'hundred Greek cities' (Hdt. 4.178-179)
left_out.reason: Legend: the oracle of Jason's tripod that a hundred Greek cities would be founded round Lake Tritonis, which the Libyans thwarted by hiding the tripod. No settlement.

left_out.name: Massaliote periplus (Avienus, Ora Maritima) and Hecataeus' Libyan towns
left_out.reason: No Greek settlement in north-west Africa is named in them; the African places they list are Libyan or Phoenician (e.g. Kanthele, 'a city of the Libyan Phoenicians', Hecataeus F 339).

left_out.name: Caput Vada (Ras Kaboudia, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Justinian made Belisarius' landing place a walled city (Procopius, Aed. 6.6.8-16), but there is no evidence of Greek-speaking residents; a Latin town under imperial rule. Out.

left_out.name: Vaga / Theodorias (Beja, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Renamed after the empress Theodora (Procopius, Aed. 6.5.14); Latin town with a garrison; no Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Sufetula (Sbeitla, Tunisia)
left_out.reason: Latin Roman town; seat of the rebel exarch Gregory, defeated and killed there by 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh in 647; no Greek-speaking civilian community attested.

left_out.name: Mauritania (whole country)
left_out.reason: No Greek settlement, Greek inscription or Greek-speaking community is recorded; the identifications of Hanno's and Ps.-Scylax's Kerne with sites on this coast are conjectures about Punic voyages.

left_out.name: Megalepolis and White Tunis (Tynes Leukos), Cap Bon and Tunis, Tunisia
left_out.reason: Punic towns taken by Agathocles in 310 BC (Diod. 20.8); 'Great City' is a Greek rendering, not a Greek foundation; no Greek settlement.

left_out.name: Garama (Germa, Fezzan, Libya)
left_out.reason: Capital of the Garamantes; Roman and Mediterranean imports only; no Greek settlement or Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Parembole (Debod), Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Temple of Amun built by the Meroitic king Adikhalamani and enlarged under the Ptolemies and Augustus, with a Roman camp (the Greek name means 'camp'); a fort and temple site in the Dodekaschoinos, not a city; no Greek-speaking civic community. The temple was moved to Madrid in 1968-1972.

left_out.name: Tzitzis (Kertassi), Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Sandstone quarry with a kiosk and many Greek inscriptions of quarry workers and soldiers (2nd-3rd c.); a quarry, not a city.

left_out.name: Talmis (Kalabsha), Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Temple town of Mandulis in the Dodekaschoinos with a Roman garrison. Its Greek texts are official or royal: soldiers' and visitors' prayers (proskynemata), the decree of Aurelius Besarion also called Ammonios, strategos of the Ombite nome and Elephantine, ordering pigs out of 'the sacred village of Talmis' (OGIS 210, AD 248/249), and the Greek victory inscription of Silko, 'king of the Nobades and all the Ethiopians' (5th or early 6th c.), written in the Greek of a Nubian court; beside them the Meroitic inscription of the king Kharamadoye. The residents spoke Egyptian, Meroitic and later Blemmye and Nobadian; no Greek civic institutions or Greek-speaking resident community are attested. Not a city with civic status.

left_out.name: Taphis (Tafa), Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Small temple and Roman fort site in the Dodekaschoinos; no civic status and no Greek-speaking community beyond soldiers.

left_out.name: Contra Pselchis (Quban, Baki), Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Fortress at the mouth of the Wadi Allaqi gold route opposite Pselchis, used from the Middle Kingdom to Roman times; a fort, not a city.

left_out.name: Pselchis (Dakka), Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Temple of Thoth of Pnubs begun by the Meroitic king Arkamani (Ergamenes) with Ptolemy IV and finished under the Romans; called a town of the Ethiopians taken by C. Petronius in 24 BC (Strabo 17.1.54). In Roman times it was a garrison post: the Greek ostraca and inscriptions are those of soldiers and visitors. No civic status and no resident Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Hiera Sykaminos (Maharraqa), Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Southern limit of the Dodekaschoinos and of Roman Egypt from Augustus to Diocletian (Ptolemy, Geography; Itinerarium Antonini), a Roman fort and station with a temple of Isis and Serapis; Greek inscriptions are those of soldiers and travellers. Diocletian withdrew the frontier to Philae in 298 (Procopius, Wars 1.19.27-37). A station, not a city.

left_out.name: Primis (Qasr Ibrim), Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Meroitic fortress town (Premnis) stormed by C. Petronius in 24 BC and held by a Roman garrison of 400 men until the settlement with the Meroites in 21/20 BC (Strabo 17.1.54); the papyri of that period found there (among them the Latin elegies of Cornelius Gallus) belong to the garrison. Later a Meroitic, Nobadian and Christian Nubian centre and episcopal see, where Greek was used in church and in some documents beside Coptic, Old Nubian and Arabic. No Greek-speaking resident community; Greek was official, military or ecclesiastical.

left_out.name: Pachoras (Faras), Northern State, Sudan (now under Lake Nubia)
left_out.reason: Capital of the Nubian kingdom of Nobadia and seat of its bishops, with the cathedral and its wall paintings; the inscriptions and captions are in Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian, and the list of bishops is in Coptic. Greek here was the language of the liturgy and of formal writing among Nubian speakers, not a spoken community language (Ochala 2014; Lajtar). Not a Greek or bilingual city in the sense used here.

left_out.name: Sai, Northern State, Sudan
left_out.reason: Island town and fortress with Pharaonic, Kushite, Meroitic and Christian remains, a Nubian bishopric in the Christian period; Greek only in ecclesiastical inscriptions. Nubian-speaking; no Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Old Dongola (Tungul), Northern State, Sudan
left_out.reason: Capital of the Nubian kingdom of Makuria, founded c. 5th c.; it withstood Arab attacks in 642 and 652, ended by the treaty (baqt) with 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh. Greek was used for liturgy, funerary epitaphs and royal titles into the 12th-14th c., beside Old Nubian and Coptic, but by Nubian speakers; scholars treat it as a written and church language, not the speech of a resident community (Lajtar; Ochala 2014). Not a Greek or bilingual city.

left_out.name: Soba, Khartoum State, Sudan
left_out.reason: Capital of the Nubian kingdom of Alodia (Alwa), converted by the mission of Longinus c. 580 (John of Ephesus, Ecclesiastical History 4.49-53); a few Greek and Old Nubian church inscriptions; Nubian-speaking, no Greek community.

left_out.name: Napata (Jebel Barkal / Karima), Northern State, Sudan
left_out.reason: Kushite royal and religious centre, sacked by C. Petronius in 24/23 BC (Strabo 17.1.54; Res Gestae 26; Pliny, NH 6.181-182); Egyptian and Meroitic in language; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Meroe (Begrawiya), River Nile State, Sudan
left_out.reason: Capital of the kingdom of Kush; Diodorus (3.6.3) says King Ergamenes had a Greek education, and Hellenistic objects and a fragmentary Greek victory inscription of a 4th-c. Aksumite king were found there; but it was a Meroitic-speaking city and Greek was known only to a few at court. No Greek-speaking community.

left_out.name: Miam (Aniba) and Karanog, Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Meroitic administrative centre of Lower Nubia, seat of the Meroitic governors (peshto) in the 2nd-3rd c., with Meroitic funerary inscriptions; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Gebel Adda, Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Meroitic, Nobadian and Christian Nubian town; Meroitic, Old Nubian and church inscriptions; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Ballana and Qustul, Aswan Governorate, Egypt
left_out.reason: Royal tombs of the Nobadian kings (4th-6th c.) with imported Roman silver and bronze; cemeteries, not cities, and no Greek community.

left_out.name: Kawa (Gematon), Northern State, Sudan
left_out.reason: Kushite temple town with Egyptian-language and Meroitic inscriptions; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Musawwarat es-Sufra and Naqa, River Nile State, Sudan
left_out.reason: Meroitic religious and royal centres (Naqa has a temple kiosk in a Roman-influenced style); Meroitic-speaking, no Greek community.

left_out.name: Elephant-hunting stations of the Trogodytic coast (Soteira Limen, Eumenes' Grove, the hunts of Pytholaos and Lichas, the Harbour of Antiphilos, Cape Pytholaos and others), Sudan and Eritrea
left_out.reason: Bases and landmarks of the Ptolemaic elephant hunts named after their commanders (Strabo 16.4.8-15; Pliny, NH 6.171-173); manned by hunters, soldiers and sailors and given up when the hunts ended in the 2nd c. BC. Stations without civic status.

left_out.name: Berenike of the Sabai, Red Sea coast (Eritrea or Sudan, unlocated)
left_out.reason: Strabo (16.4.10, after Artemidorus) names 'Berenike, a Sabaean city' and 'Sabai, a good-sized city' on the African coast south of Ptolemais; a Ptolemaic name for a place in a native region, with no evidence of Greek settlers or civic life and no located remains.

left_out.name: Sabai, Red Sea coast (Eritrea or Sudan, unlocated)
left_out.reason: Native town called 'a good-sized city' by Strabo (16.4.10); no Greek community.
