left_out.name: Arsinoe near Deire, near Assab, Southern Red Sea Region, Eritrea (unlocated)
left_out.reason: A Ptolemaic Arsinoe just before the strait of Deire, 'a city and harbour' in Strabo (16.4.14, after Artemidorus), also in Pliny (NH 6.170) and Ptolemy (Geography 4.7) (Pleiades 39295); known only from geographers' lists, with no evidence of Greek settlers, civic life or excavated remains. Probably a station of the hunting and naval network. Rejected for lack of positive evidence; doubtful.

left_out.name: Berenike Epi Deires, Ras Siyan (Obock Region, Djibouti) or near Assab (Eritrea)
left_out.reason: Pliny (NH 6.170) counts 'Berenice Epi Dires' among the Ptolemaic Berenices, Ptolemy (Geography 4.7) lists Deire as a city, and Artemidorus (in Strabo 16.4.4) knows at the strait a town of the same name 'inhabited by Ichthyophagi'. The name shows a Ptolemaic foundation or renaming, but no Greek settlers, civic institutions, inscriptions or remains are attested and the site is unexcavated. Rejected for lack of positive evidence of a Greek community; doubtful.

left_out.name: Adulis (Zula), Northern Red Sea Region, Eritrea
left_out.reason: Port of Aksum. Pliny (NH 6.172) tells that runaway Egyptian slaves founded it (a tale built on the name); the Periplus (4) calls it a fair-sized village and a lawful market, and says King Zoskales knew Greek letters (5). Its Greek texts are royal: Ptolemy III's victory inscription (which may point to a Ptolemaic hunting station there in the 3rd c. BC, i.e. soldiers and hunters, not settlers) and the Greek inscription of an Aksumite king (Monumentum Adulitanum), both copied c. 518-525 by Cosmas Indicopleustes at the request of the governor of Adulis under King Kaleb. Roman merchants came and went by sea (Cosmas was one of them), and imported amphorae, Roman wares and a Menas flask are found, but no inscriptions, ostraca, clergy or institutions of a resident Greek-speaking community are known. The town was abandoned in the late 6th or 7th c. (Zazzaro 2014; the traditional Arab raid of 640 is unproven). Greek was a royal and trade language here, not a community language.

left_out.name: Aksum (Axum), Tigray Region, Ethiopia
left_out.reason: Capital of the Aksumite kingdom. Greek was used in royal inscriptions (the Greek versions of King Ezana's inscriptions, c. 330-360, beside Ge'ez in Ethiopic and in South Arabian script) and on coin legends from c. 270 to the early 7th c.; but it was a royal, diplomatic and trade language. Rufinus (Ecclesiastical History 10.9-10) tells that Frumentius, a Greek from Tyre at the court, gathered the Roman merchants staying in the kingdom into Christian meeting places (c. 330s): a small foreign merchant colony, not a community that made Greek one of the city's main languages. The people spoke Ge'ez; no Greek civic institutions or Greek-speaking civic community are attested.

left_out.name: Koloe (Qohaito), Southern Region, Eritrea
left_out.reason: Inland town and ivory market of the Periplus (4) and Ptolemy (Geography 4.7); an Aksumite town with Ge'ez and Sabaic remains; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Matara, Southern Region, Eritrea
left_out.reason: Aksumite town near Senafe excavated by F. Anfray (from 1959), with a Ge'ez inscription on a stela and Aksumite coins; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Avalites (probably Zeila, Awdal, Somaliland, Somalia; some propose a site near Assab, Eritrea)
left_out.reason: Small market of the 'far-side' coast (Periplus 7), where goods were brought on rafts and small boats; under local chiefs (Periplus 14). A native emporion visited by Greek-speaking merchants from Egypt; no Greek residents or civic status.

left_out.name: Malao (Berbera, Sahil, Somaliland, Somalia)
left_out.reason: Market of the Periplus (8), an open roadstead whose natives were 'more peaceable'; a native emporion visited by traders from Egypt; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Mundu (probably Heis/Xiis, Sanaag, Somaliland, Somalia)
left_out.reason: Market of the Periplus (9) on an offshore island; native emporion; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Mosylon (near Bosaso or Ras Hantara, Bari, Puntland, Somalia)
left_out.reason: Market of the Periplus (10) exporting cassia; native emporion; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Spice Market (Aromaton Emporion), near Cape Guardafui (Damo), Bari, Somalia
left_out.reason: Market and anchorage of the Periplus (12); native emporion; no Greek community.

left_out.name: Opone (Ras Hafun), Bari, Somalia
left_out.reason: Market of the Periplus (13) for cinnamon and slaves; excavations by N. Chittick (1975) and later work found occupation from about the 1st c. BC to the 5th c. AD with Roman amphorae and wares; a native trading settlement visited by Mediterranean merchants; no Greek residents or civic status.

left_out.name: Sarapion and Nikon, Benadir coast, Somalia
left_out.reason: Names of anchorages on the 'courses of Azania' given by Greek-speaking sailors (Periplus 15; Ptolemy, Geography 1.17); not settlements of Greeks.

left_out.name: Rhapta (unlocated: Rufiji delta or Pangani, Tanzania)
left_out.reason: The last market of Azania (Periplus 16; Ptolemy, Geography 1.9, 4.7, the 'metropolis' of Barbaria); governed for the king of the Himyarites through the chief of Mapharitis, and its trade was in the hands of Arab merchants from Muza who married local women and knew the language (Periplus 16). No Greek community.

left_out.name: Menouthias (Pemba, Zanzibar or Mafia, Tanzania)
left_out.reason: Island of the Periplus (15) inhabited by native fishermen; no Greek presence beyond passing ships.

left_out.name: Pyralaon islands and the Channel (Lamu archipelago, Lamu County, Kenya)
left_out.reason: Islands of the Periplus (15) on the Azanian coast, with native inhabitants; no Greek presence beyond passing ships.

left_out.name: Dioskorides (Socotra)
left_out.reason: Outside the area: Socotra belongs to Yemen. The Periplus (30) mentions Greek traders among its mixed population and Cosmas (3.65) Greek-speaking Christian settlers.

left_out.name: Phagroriopolis (Phagroriopolite nome)
left_out.reason: Strabo 17.1.26 names the Phagroriopolite nome and its city on the canal to the Red Sea (eastern Delta, near the Wadi Tumilat); unlocated, absent from Ptolemy, Hierocles and the bishop lists, and no Greek civic evidence; a nome capital of the early Roman period that never shows up as a city.

left_out.name: Anthylla
left_out.reason: Town near Naukratis whose revenue paid for the queen's shoes under the Persians (Hdt. 2.97-98; Athenaeus 1.33d on its wine); no civic status, nome, see or Greek civic evidence.

left_out.name: Archandroupolis
left_out.reason: Town named only by Herodotus (2.97-98) on the road from Naukratis to Memphis; unlocated, no later evidence (sometimes linked with Andropolis, which is entered).

left_out.name: Kerkasoros (Kerkesoura)
left_out.reason: Village at the head of the Delta (Hdt. 2.15, 2.17; Strabo 17.1.4); no civic status.

left_out.name: Platea (island off the Gulf of Bomba, Libya)
left_out.reason: First seat of the Theraean colonists under Battos for two years (Hdt. 4.151-157), before they moved to Aziris on the mainland and then to Cyrene (631 BC); a camp of the colonists, not a city. Greek pottery on the island.

stories.title: The Museum and the Library
stories.text: Founded by Alexander in 331 BC, the capital of the Ptolemies drew the scholars of the Greek world to its Museum and Library. Euclid wrote the Elements here, Eratosthenes ran the Library, Hero built his machines and Claudius Ptolemy wrote the Almagest. The Jewish Law was first put into Greek here, the beginning of the Septuagint, and the Pharos lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders. The philosopher Hypatia taught here until a Christian mob killed her in 415.

stories.title: Two women at the festival of Adonis
stories.text: In Theocritus' fifteenth Idyll (270s BC) two Syracusan housewives living in Alexandria, Gorgo and Praxinoa, push through the crowded streets to the palace, where Queen Arsinoe II is holding the festival of Adonis. They grumble about their husbands, admire the tapestries and snap at a stranger who mocks their Doric vowels, then hear a singer's hymn to Adonis.

stories.title: The pleasure philosophers
stories.text: Aristippus of Cyrene, a companion of Socrates, taught that the good is the pleasure of the moment, and is counted the founder of the Cyrenaic school. He taught his daughter Arete, and she taught her son, Aristippus, called 'the mother-taught'. Later Cyrenaics went further: Theodorus 'the Atheist' denied the gods, and Hegesias argued so well that life is not worth living that a King Ptolemy is said to have forbidden him to teach it, because his hearers killed themselves (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 1.83).

stories.title: Callimachus, Eratosthenes, Carneades
stories.text: Cyrene gave Alexandria some of its greatest scholars. The poet Callimachus (c. 305–240 BC), who claimed descent from the city's founder Battos, catalogued Greek literature in the 120 books of his Pinakes and wrote that 'a big book is a big evil'. Eratosthenes (c. 276–194 BC) became head of the Library. Carneades (214–129 BC) led Plato's Academy in Athens; sent to Rome in 155 BC, he spoke for justice one day and against it the next, and Cato had the embassy sent home. Earlier, Theodorus of Cyrene had shown that the square roots of 3, 5 and the other numbers up to 17 that are not squares are irrational (Plato, Theaetetus 147d).

stories.title: Cyrene in Pindar
stories.text: Pindar wrote three victory odes for men of Cyrene. The longest of all his odes, the Fourth Pythian (462 BC), celebrates the chariot victory of King Arkesilas IV and tells the story of the Argonauts and of the founding of Cyrene by Battos, the descendant of an Argonaut, on the Delphic oracle's command.

stories.title: Synesius, bishop and philosopher
stories.text: Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–c. 414), a pupil of the philosopher Hypatia at Alexandria, became bishop of Ptolemais in 410 on condition that he could keep his wife and his philosophy. His letters describe the defence of the city against nomad raids.

stories.title: Where Eratosthenes measured the Earth
stories.text: Syene was thought to lie on the tropic: at noon on the summer solstice the sun stood straight overhead and lit the water of a well (Strabo 17.1.48). Eratosthenes of Cyrene found that at Alexandria, on the same day, the sun stood a fiftieth of a circle from the zenith. Taking Syene to be 5,000 stadia away, he made the circumference of the Earth 250,000 stadia (Cleomedes): close to the true figure, though how close depends on the length of his stadion.

stories.title: Nonnos and the poets of Panopolis
stories.text: Nonnos of Panopolis wrote the Dionysiaca in the 5th century AD: 48 books, as many as the Iliad and the Odyssey together, and some 21,000 lines of Greek hexameters on the god Dionysus, the longest poem to survive from Greek and Roman antiquity. He also put the Gospel of John into hexameters. That this vast epic came from a man of a town deep in Upper Egypt, where most people spoke Coptic, is one of the surprises of Greek literature. Panopolis gave its age a whole school of Greek poets, among them Cyrus and Pamprepius; a century earlier it had produced the alchemist Zosimos.

stories.title: The Greeks' port in Egypt
stories.text: Herodotus tells that Charaxus, the brother of the poet Sappho, bought the freedom of the courtesan Rhodopis at Naukratis, and that nine cities of the East Greeks built a common sanctuary here, the Hellenion (Herodotus 2.135, 2.178; Strabo 17.1.33). Naukratis later gave Greek literature Athenaeus (c. AD 200), whose Deipnosophists, a dinner-party conversation in fifteen books, preserves quotations from hundreds of lost works.

stories.title: The poet of the Argonauts?
stories.text: Apollonius, the author of the Argonautica, the epic of Jason and the Golden Fleece, was head of the Library at Alexandria before Eratosthenes. His ancient Lives call him an Alexandrian, but Athenaeus (7.283d) and Aelian say he came from Naukratis. Why he was called 'of Rhodes' is uncertain.

stories.title: A leap year before Caesar
stories.text: In March 238 BC the priests of Egypt met at Canopus and passed a decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek in honour of Ptolemy III and Berenike II. It added a day to every fourth year, so that the festivals would stop drifting through the seasons, two centuries before Julius Caesar; the reform was not kept. A copy was found at Tanis in 1866.

stories.title: Solon and Atlantis
stories.text: Plato has Solon visit Sais, the city of the pharaohs of the 26th dynasty, where an old priest told him that 'you Greeks are always children' and that Athens had once defeated Atlantis (Timaeus 21e–25d).

stories.title: The skulls of Pelusium
stories.text: At Pelusium, the gate of Egypt, the Persian king Cambyses defeated the Egyptians in 525 BC. Herodotus saw the bones still lying in two heaps on the battlefield, and was told that Persian skulls could be pierced with a pebble while Egyptian skulls could hardly be broken with a stone (Herodotus 3.12).

stories.title: The decree on the Rosetta Stone
stories.text: Greeks and Carians lived in their own quarters at Memphis from the 6th century BC. In 196 BC the priests of Egypt, gathered at Memphis, passed a decree in honour of the young Ptolemy V, to be set up in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. A copy found at Rosetta in 1799 gave the key to the hieroglyphs.

stories.title: Faces of the Fayum
stories.text: Krokodilopolis was the capital of the Fayum, the province Ptolemy II named after his sister and queen Arsinoe; the town later took her name too. From the cemeteries of the Fayum come most of the mummy portraits of the 1st to 3rd centuries AD: painted faces of its townspeople, some with their names in Greek, among the few painted portraits to survive from antiquity.

stories.title: The rubbish mounds of Oxyrhynchus
stories.text: From the winter of 1896–97 Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt dug the town's rubbish mounds and found hundreds of thousands of papyri: the letters, contracts and school exercises of its families, lost works of Sappho, Pindar, Menander and Sophocles, and some of the earliest copies of the Gospels. The series they began, The Oxyrhynchus Papyri, has reached 88 volumes.

stories.title: Hadrian's city for Antinous
stories.text: Hadrian founded Antinoopolis in 130 on the bank of the Nile where his favourite, the young Bithynian Antinous, had drowned. It was a Greek city with the laws of Naukratis, settlers from Ptolemais Hermiou and the Fayum, and games in honour of Antinous.

stories.title: Plotinus
stories.text: Plotinus (205–270), the founder of Neoplatonism, was born at Lycopolis according to Eunapius. He studied philosophy at Alexandria for eleven years under Ammonius Saccas before teaching in Rome. His Enneads, edited by his pupil Porphyry, shaped pagan, Christian and Muslim thought for a thousand years.

stories.title: Ptolemy's birthplace?
stories.text: Claudius Ptolemy, the author of the Almagest and the Geography, worked at Alexandria in the 2nd century AD, and his dated observations were made there. Where he was born is unknown: only Theodore Meliteniotes, an astronomer at Constantinople around 1360, says it was Ptolemais Hermiou, the Greek city Ptolemy I had founded in Upper Egypt. The claim is late, but it could be right.

stories.title: The singing statue
stories.text: Greek and Roman visitors crossed the river from Thebes to hear the northern colossus of Memnon, a giant statue of the pharaoh Amenhotep III, 'sing' at dawn, and cut more than a hundred poems and notes on its legs. Julia Balbilla, who came with the emperor Hadrian in 130, left her verses in the Aeolic Greek of Sappho.

stories.title: Elephants and pepper
stories.text: Ptolemy II founded Berenike on the Red Sea (c. 275 BC) to bring war elephants from the African coast. Under Rome it became a port of the trade with India: excavations have found Indian pepper, teak and a statue of the Buddha.

greek_communities_after_1800.start: A Greek Orthodox community is attested from the 16th-17th centuries; in the 19th century it grew with merchants and with sponge divers from the Dodecanese. Two Chiot boys enslaved in 1822, the Khaznadar brothers, rose high at the court of the beys: Mustapha Khaznadar (Georgios Kalkias Stravelakis) became prime minister.
